tours. When visitor studies are conducted at individual parks, these unique situations are taken into account. 

Multipliers for local regions around national parks were applied to the spending totals to translate spending into jobs, income, and value added and also to estimate secondary effects. All MGM2 multipliers were re-estimated last year using IMPLAN ver 3.0 and 2008 economic data (Minnesota IMPLAN Group 2009). The multipliers have been adjusted to 2010 based on structural changes in the national IMPLAN models between 2008 and 2009 and price changes between 2009 and 2010. 

Based on national IMPLAN models, there were some significant structural changes in economic ratios and multipliers between 2008 and 2009. Most notable, was a change in ratios for the amusements sector (IMPLAN sector 410) due to an inflated estimate of output in 2008. IMPLAN ratios in 2009 for sector 410 were more than double the 2008 estimates. This caused a significant underestimate of jobs, income and value added in the MGM2 amusements sector estimates last year. In addition, there were increases of 15-30% in the ratios for retail trade sectors between 2008 and 2009. Ratios for the hotel sector (IMPLAN sector 411) declined by roughly 10%. The MGM2 estimates of jobs, income and value added are sensitive to any changes in these ratios and multipliers. 

With the exception of parks with new visitor surveys in 2010, no changes were made in party sizes, lengths of stay, or re-entry factors between 2009 and 2010. MGM2 model parameters for individual parks are adjusted over time as new park visitor studies are conducted or other relevant information becomes available. 

Impacts of park payrolls were estimated for each park by applying local area multipliers to NPS wage and salary figures for FY 2010. Multipliers capture the induced effects of park employee spending by re-circulating their income as household spending within the local economy. Payroll benefits (e.g. contributions to retirement and health insurance) were not re-circulated in estimating secondary effects of park employee spending, but the direct payroll benefits are included in total value added. Multipliers for IMPLAN sector 439 (federal government payroll) were applied to wages and salaries at each park to estimate induced effects. 15 Local impacts of park purchases of supplies and services or construction activities were not included in the analysis. 

The number of employees for each park was estimated by totaling the number of distinct social security numbers in each pay period and dividing by the number of pay periods. The figure is therefore an annual average. Four seasonal jobs for three months count as one job. No distinction is made between part-time and full-time employees. Jobs, salary, and payroll benefits are assigned to the park where the employee’s time was charged, which may differ from their duty station. 

Spending and impact totals for states were developed from the 2010 estimates by summing the results for all units in a given state using the mailing address for the park to identify the state. Twenty parks have facilities in more than one state. For these parks, visitors and spending were

12 

allocated to individual states based on shares used by the NPS Public Use Statistics Office for allocating visits to states. For example, visits to Great Smoky Mountains NP were split 44% to North Carolina and 56% to Tennessee. It should be noted that these allocations may not fully account for where the spending and impacts occur. There are also many other parks with facilities in a single state but located within 60 miles of a state border. A portion of the spending and impacts for these parks may accrue to nearby states. 

# Errors and Limitations 

The accuracy of the spending and impact estimates rests largely on the input data, namely (1) public use recreation visit and overnight stay data; (2) party size, length of stay, and park re-entry conversion factors; (3) visitor segment shares; (4) spending averages; and (5) local area multipliers. 

Public use data provides reasonably accurate estimates of visitor entries for most parks. Some visitors may be missed by the counting procedures, while others may be counted multiple times when they re-enter a park more than once on a single trip. Accurate estimates of park re-entries, party sizes, and lengths of stay in the area are needed to convert park entries to the number of visitor or party days in the region. Visitors staying overnight outside the park pose significant problems as they tend to be the greatest spenders and may enter the park several times during their stay. Similarly, visitors staying inside the park may enter and leave several times during their stay and be counted each time as a distinct visit. Re-entry factors adjust for these problems to the extent possible. 

For multi-purpose trips, it is difficult to determine what portion of the spending should be attributed to the park visit. This is especially a problem for historic sites and parks in urban areas or parks in multiple-attraction destinations. For parks with visitor surveys, the proportion of days and spending counted was decided based on stated trip purposes and the importance of the park in generating the trip to the region. 

Parkways and urban parks pose special difficulties for economic impact analyses. These units have some of the highest number of visits while posing the most difficult problems for estimating visits, spending, and impacts. The majority of visits to these types of units were assumed to be local or non-local day trips, and only one night of spending was counted for overnight trips. Due to the high numbers of visits at these units, small changes in assumed spending averages or segment mixes can swing the spending estimates by substantial amounts. 

Clusters of parks within a single 60-mile area pose additional difficulties. For example, the many monuments and parks in the Washington, D.C., area each count visitors separately. Similar difficulties exist for clusters of parks in Boston, New York, and San Francisco. To avoid double counting of spending across many national capital parks, we must know how many times a visitor has been counted at park units during a trip to the Washington, D.C., area. For parks in the National Capital Region, we currently assume an average of 1.7 park visits are counted for local day trips, 3.4 visits for non-local day trips, and 5.1 park visits on overnight trips. The non-local visitor spending total for the National Capital Region in 2010 was $1.17 billion. This is 14% of the Travel Industry Association tourist spending estimate of $8.3 billion for Washington, D.C., in 2008 (USTA 2010). 13 

NPS units in Alaska also pose special problems for economic analysis. Spending opportunities near Alaska parks are limited and for many visitors the park visit is part of a cruise or guided tour, frequently purchased as a package. Most visitors are on extended trips to Alaska, making it difficult to allocate expenses to a particular park visit. Lodging, vehicle rentals, and air expenses frequently occur in Anchorage, many miles from the park. Also, many Alaska parks are only accessible by air or boat, so spending profiles estimated from visitor surveys at parks in the lower 48 states do not apply well. Due to the prominence of cruise lines and package tours, special studies are required to estimate the proportion of visitor spending that stays in the local regions around national park units in Alaska. In this report, Alaska statewide multipliers are used to estimate impacts for parks in Alaska. 

A visit to one or more national parks is an important part of the trip for most Alaska visitors. One could therefore argue to count a substantial portion of tourism spending in Alaska as related to national park visits. The U.S. Travel Association estimated tourist spending in Alaska at $2.1 billion in 2008 (USTA 2010). This is ten times what we have included as spending by park visitors in the local regions around Alaska national parks. Including spending in Alaska outside the local regions would significantly increase the estimates; however, deciding which spending to include would be somewhat subjective. 15

iv Economic Impacts of Timed-Entry Reservation System at Arches National Park 

gardner.utah.edu I April 2026 I N F O R M E D D E C I S I O N S TM 1Analysis in Brief 

Grand County, Utah experienced positive economic impacts and growth in average annual visitor-generated tax revenue after implementation of a timed-entry reservation system at Arches National Park (Arches) in 2022. 

Visitation 

While visitation to Arches remained relatively flat between 2022 and 2024 (0.4% increase), statistical analysis indicates that the timed-entry system likely reduced Arches visitation relative to a counterfactual Arches baseline with no timed-entry system. 

Visitor Spending 

Had no other changes occurred, the visitation reduction would likely have led to foregone visitor spending in the years since implementation (2022–2024). However, potential foregone visitor spending from the timed-entry system appears more than offset by higher spending within Grand County from business travelers and visitors to Arches and other nearby national and state parks, and from those drawn to Grand County’s beautiful landscapes and diverse recreational opportunities outside of those parks. 

Economy 

Since 2022, Grand County’s economy experienced positive growth, as measured by jobs, total wages, and other standard economic indicators. A range of factors beyond timed entry also influenced Grand County's economy, making timed entry's effect more uncertain. 

Key Findings • Grand County’s Visitor Economy – Tourism jobs in Grand County increased 16.3% post–timed-entry (2022–2024 average), relative to pre–timed-entry (2017–2019 average). Adjusting for inflation, visitor spending and visitor-generated tax revenue increased 22.2% and 27.8% respectively. However, both visitor spending and visitor-generated tax revenue declined slightly between 2022 and 2024. 

• Arches Timed-Entry System – The timed-entry system reduced Arches visitation by an estimated 170,000 people (14.1% reduction from estimated counterfactual totals) on average per year between 2022 and 2024. 

• Foregone Visitor Spending and Local Fiscal Impacts – 

Had no other changes occurred, reduced visitation would have led to between $41.4 and $55.1 million of foregone annual visitor spending (9% to 11% reduction from estimated counterfactual totals) in Grand County. Local net fiscal impacts (revenues less expenditures) associated with this foregone spending range from negative $1.9–$2.6 million in 2022 to negative $2.0–$2.7 million in 2024, meaning estimated lost tax revenue exceeds cost savings. 

• Grand County’s Positive Economic Outcomes – 

A combination of factors since implementation of the timed-entry system at Arches—including a possible change in the composition of visitors to Arches, increased visitors at Canyonlands National Park and Dead Horse Point State Park, and the availability of other recreational and business activities in the county—also influenced Grand County's economy, making timed entry's effect on broader economic outcomes more uncertain.

# Introduction 

In 2022, the National Park Service implemented a timed-entry reservation system at Arches National Park (Arches) in Grand County, Utah. This analysis explores Grand County’s economic and visitation impacts since then. While visitation to Arches remained relatively flat between 2022 and 2024 (0.4% increase), statistical analysis indicates that the timed-entry system likely reduced Arches visitation relative to a counterfactual baseline with no timed-entry system. The visitation reduction would have led to foregone visitor spending estimated between $41.4 million and $55.1 million annually in the years since implementation (2022–2024), all else equal. However, potential foregone visitor spending from the timed-entry system appears more than offset by higher actual spending within Grand County from business travelers and visitors to Arches and other nearby national and state parks, and from those drawn to Grand County’s stunning landscapes and diverse recreational opportunities outside of those parks. Grand County is home to two of Utah’s five national parks—Arches and a portion of Canyonlands—as well as two state parks—Utahraptor and a portion of Dead Horse Point (Figure 1). Since 2022, Grand County’s economy experienced positive growth, as measured by jobs, total wages, and other economic indicators. While varying by economic indicator, a range of analytical approaches signals positive economic impacts countywide, relative to a counterfactual Grand County that assumes no timed entry at Arches. The pre–timed-entry system analysis for this report includes years 2017 to 2019, omitting 2020 and 2021 because of anomalous conditions during that time related to the COVID-19 pandemic. The post–timed-entry system analysis focuses on years 2022 through 2024. While visitation data and some economic data for 2025 are now available at the time of publication, these data were not available during the project’s research phase. Also of note, 2025 presents a unique data year due to the federal government shutdown during October and November, which reduced staffing at Arches and eliminated the timed-entry system earlier than normal.

# Timed-Entry Background 

Since 2017, seven U.S. national parks (including Arches) and one national monument introduced timed-entry or vehicle reservation systems to manage congestion, enhance visitor experiences, and protect natural resources (Table 1). Haleakalā National Park in Hawaii first implemented a reservation system (2017) to manage visitor traffic entering the park during early morning hours for sunrise viewing. Other parks soon followed: Muir Woods National Monument launched a permanent parking and shuttle reservation system in 2018; Acadia National Park (2020) piloted a reservation requirement for Cadillac Summit Road, which the park permanently implemented in 2021; and Rocky Mountain National Park piloted a timed-entry reservation system in 2020 (following four years of testing a first-come/first-served park entry system). That same year (2020), Yosemite National Park tested multiple timed-entry systems and has since maintained limited entry reservations during peak seasons, weekends, and holidays. In 2024, Glacier and Mount Rainier National Parks launched timed-entry pilots, which they maintained with some adjustments in 2025. Arches National Park piloted a timed-entry system from April to October from 2022 to 2024, adjusting it in 2025 with staggered dates and limited entry hours. In early 2026, the National Park Service announced it would not use the timed-entry system at Arches in 2026. 1 Previous studies explore the Arches timed-entry system and its effects while other related literature provide context to Arches and park visitation generally. See Appendix A for additional details. Across all parks, the design of timed-entry and vehicle registration systems controls visitation during high-use periods, requires small non-refundable processing fees, and relies on advance, online reservations. Most systems open bookings months in advance, with limited release closer to entry. 2 Timed-entry windows regulate arrival periods but generally allow visitors to stay once inside, and early-morning or late-evening entry (outside of reservation hours) remains unrestricted in most cases. While national park reservation systems share objectives, they vary in scope, seasonality, and complexity. 3Reservation coverage also differs by park, from regulating access to specific roads or corridors to covering full-park entry. 4Park administrative models and fees also range widely. 5 Overall, U.S. national park reservation systems reflect the National Park Service’s evolving strategy to balance access and preservation through adaptive visitor management. 6

Visitation varies by park and across time, with most national parks and Utah state parks experiencing visitation growth before and after COVID-19–affected years. 7 Visitation dropped during 2020 but rebounded in 2021 at most parks. A timed-entry system often correlates with reduced overall visitation— not just peak hour visitation—as seen at Arches and elsewhere (Figure 2). Arches represents the only national park in Utah without significant positive visitation growth between 2022 and 2024 (Figure 3). No other national park in Utah implemented a timed-entry system to date. Notably, visitation increased between 2022 and 2024 at Canyonlands National Park and Dead Horse Point State Park, both in Grand County and without any timed-entry system, suggesting the possibility of substitution behavior among visitors to Grand County (away from Arches and towards alternative parks) during years with timed entry in place (Table 2, Figure 4). After a modest dip from 2019 to 2022, total visitation across these Grand County parks continued to grow in 2023 and 2024. Monthly visitation data exhibit seasonality, as expected. However, of note, the offseason counts and share of total annual visitation generally increased in the last 10 to 15 years for most national parks. Following implementation of the Arches timed-entry system, Grand County’s visitor economy expanded overall, though with mixed accommodation performance. Average hotel capacity grew by 18.9% between 2017–2019 and 2022–2024, while occupancy rates declined modestly from 78.9% to 75.1%, indicating the market absorbed most of the new room supply. Additionally, the average number of hotel rooms occupied increased by 13.2%, reflecting continued demand growth. While nominal average daily rates (ADR) and revenue per available room (RevPAR) rose over this period, inflation-adjusted ADR was flat, and RevPAR declined, suggesting some compression in revenue per room. These accommodation trends are consistent with broader regional patterns among Utah’s rural national park gateway counties. In contrast, the short-term rental sector expanded more rapidly and achieved occupied room night and pricing gains despite lower occupancy rates. This highlights nightly rate growth along with inventory expansion. For additional details related to Grand County’s accommodation sector, see Appendix C. Beyond lodging, visitor spending and related tax revenues both increased in real (inflation-adjusted) terms, and total private-sec-tor, public-sector and tourism employment grew (Table 3). Taken together, the data indicate positive visitor economy outcomes in Grand County post–timed-entry, marked by supply growth and continued expansion in overall visitor economic activity.

While the previous sections illustrate trends in visitation, visitor spending, and other indicators, those analyses do not equate correlation to causation. In this section and the following section, the statistical analysis seeks to quantify the causal effect, if any, of timed-entry at Arches on subsequent visitation. The park-level statistical analysis estimates the visitation that Arches would have experienced without timed entry beginning in 2022. The authors estimate this counterfactual outcome using an empirical technique called synthetic control. This analysis approximates, as closely as possible, a “parallel” or “counterfactual” version of Arches, similar in all relevant ways to the actual Arches National Park but without timed entry. The difference in visitation between the actual and parallel versions of Arches approximates the effects of timed entry. Synthetic control estimates Arches visitation without timed entry as a weighted average of the visitation of other national parks that were similar to Arches prior to 2022 but that do not have timed-entry systems. For a complete list of candidate parks, see Appendix F. The synthetic control algorithm assigns weights to candidate parks, where those with non-zero weights become "control" parks. Since control parks closely predict Arches visitation before timed entry (with actual Arches visitation nearly identical to counterfactual Arches), then they should continue to closely predict counterfactual Arches after timed-entry implementation at Arches. The model specification controls for various potential explanatory factors of visitation, such as gasoline prices, weather, the population of the nearest population center, and other factors to isolate the effect of timed entry. This park-level analysis follows—in method and various implementation details—a recent study of the effects of the Mighty 5 ad campaign on visitation at Utah’s national parks. 8 Appendix E provides further details on the methodology of synthetic control. The timed-entry system at Arches National Park decreased park visitation, with estimated declines of 13.7% (200,000 visits) in 2022, 16.5% (244,000 visits) in 2023, and 19.0% (279,000 visits) in 2024. This analysis divides the number of lost visits by 1.41, the average number of visits to the park by each visitor, to yield the number of lost visitors. 9Table 7 shows the differences in visitation between Arches and counterfactual Arches for 2022 to 2024. In addition to these estimated differences, the uncertainty range (middle 50%) reflects a range of estimates based on the interquartile range of estimates from 30 model variations. Appendix F discusses these model variations.

Statistical Definitions Synthetic control – Synthetic control represents a weighted average of characteristics from other, non-treated units, forming a hypothetical unit for comparison. In this report, other units consist of other parks and counties (not Arches or Grand County). Synthetic controls estimate counterfactual visitation at Arches and counterfactual economic outcomes in Grand County, had timed-entry not been implemented in 2022. To simplify terminology, this report uses the term “counterfactual” to refer to either a synthetic control or an estimated counterfactual outcome. 

Statistical significance – A statistically significant difference in measured outcomes is one large enough to confidently say it reflects a true difference in the underlying unmeasurable outcomes; a difference that is not statistically significant is too small to detect with confidence, given random variation in observable data. 

Interquartile or uncertainty range – The interquartile range refers to the middle 50% of data, meaning data points falling between the 25 th and 75 th percentiles. This does not represent a confidence interval. Here, the shaded region in Figure 7 represents the interquartile range of 30 different estimates for estimating counterfactual visits at Arches from 30 unique model specifications. An estimate may fall outside the range, meaning the estimate was somewhat less typical (less than the 25th percentile or greater than the 75th percentile of all estimates). Results tables 7 and 11 through 14 refer to the interquartile range as the uncertainty range. For additional details, see Appendix F.

Data and Sources 

This analysis relies on two datasets, built from acombination of federal and state data, as well as other public sources, to conduct statistical modeling of the economic impacts resulting from the implementation of the timed-entry system at Arches National Park. The first dataset contains park-level data for all national parks in the U.S. The second dataset contains county-level data for Grand County, and all other counties in the U.S. with a national park. Where possible, data begins in 1990 and continues at annual frequency until the most recent year of available data. The park-level dataset contains park characteristics such as size, timed-entry status, budget, number of entrances, and capacity, as well as other control variables that could explain visitation data changes such as price of gasoline, a weather-related variable, and other data. Visitation counts represent outcome data for the first set of statistical models. The county-level dataset contains county characteristics such as size, population, percentage of adult population with a college degree, urban/rural status, etc., as well as economic data related to income and wages, employment and unemployment, taxable sales, and other indicators. Six of the economic variables serve as outcome variables in the statistical modeling. Appendix D summarizes all data (Tables D1 and D2), along with details of their geographic coverage, time-period coverage, and available frequency.

The forgone annual park visits estimated previously in this section could represent lost visitor spending in and around Arches National Park. The Gardner Institute estimates that, all else equal, forgone visitor spending could range from $34.4– $45.9 million in 2022 to $47.7–$63.5 million in 2024 (in inflation-adjusted 2025 dollars) (Table 10). The statistical analysis does not align with observed data trends because the “all else equal” assumption does not completely hold true. For example, rather than maintaining an identical visitor profile as the “all else equal” assumption holds, the timed-entry system could have changed the composition of visitors in reality, with fewer casual day-trippers and more intentional visitors who plan well in advance and might spend more time and money in Grand County. Further research should explore these potential visitor profile changes. See the Conclusion for author recommendations. Holding other assumptions in the economy constant (ceteris paribus conditions)—such as visitor profile, visitor behavior, ignoring substitution effects, etc.—results in negative economic and fiscal impacts. See Appendix G for the ceteris paribus analysis. A credible synthetic control for visitation at Arches should closely resemble Arches prior to the beginning of the timed-entry system (2022). Table 9 shows annual visitation for Arches, average annual visitation in the full sample of national parks without timed-entry (“All-Park Average”), and the annual visitation for synthetic (counterfactual) Arches. In general, characteristics of synthetic Arches more closely match actual pre–timed-entry Arches than does the full sample of national parks. For example, annual visitation from 1990–1997 averages 776,848 for Arches, 613,540 (27% lower than actual) for the full sample of national parks, and 842,391 for the synthetic control (8% above actual). Visitation in the other three historical periods follows similar patterns. Only one case—gasoline prices—shows the full-sample average closer than the synthetic control but the difference is small and gas prices receive only a very small weight (i.e., they were not very useful for predicting historical visitation 1990–2021 above and beyond the other variables). The best-fitting synthetic control for park visitation consists of Canyonlands (36.2%), Zion (24.0%), Joshua Tree (18.6%), Bryce Canyon (11.4%), Theodore Roosevelt National Park (4.9%), Wrangell–St. Elias National Park (2.9%), Yellowstone (1.2%), and a few others with weights less than 1% (Table 8). 

# County-Level Economic Analysis 

The county-level statistical analysis estimates the economic outcomes Grand County would have experienced without the initiation of the Arches timed-entry system in 2022. As in the park visitation analysis, the authors employ synthetic control modeling to estimate these counterfactual outcomes. This widely deployed method provided the basis for two studies on the effects of national monument designations on host county per capita income—including analyses of Utah’s Garfield and Kane counties. These studies serve as helpful guides for the analysis of Grand County. 10,11 This analysis approximates, as closely as possible, a “parallel” or “counterfactual” version of Grand County, identical in all relevant ways to actual Grand County but without timed entry at Arches National Park. The difference in economic outcomes between the actual and parallel versions of Grand County approximates the effects of timed entry on those outcomes. Synthetic control estimates Grand County outcomes without timed entry as a weighted average of the outcomes of other counties that were similar to Grand County prior to 2022 but that do not host national parks with timed-entry systems. Since control counties closely predict Grand County economic outcomes before timed entry (when actual Grand County is nearly identical to counterfactual Grand County), they should continue to closely predict counterfactual Grand County after timed entry at Arches. The model specification controls for various potential explanatory factors of economic outcomes, such as educational attainment, urban/rural status, population, and other county factors to isolate the effect of timed entry. To the extent the Arches timed-entry system reduced visitation and to the extent people instead visited other parks in Grand County, or other county attractions, the county-level analysis captures those effects. Known as “substitution effects,” one activity substitutes for another based on individual preferences and choices. However, the county-level analysis cannot control for every known event that could have increased economic outcomes after implementation of the timed-entry system. 

Model Results 

The analysis assessed the impact of timed entry on six economic outcomes: job counts, total wages, average wages, total income, income per capita, and the unemployment rate. Appendix F contains results for total income and income per capita, along with additional details for each economic outcome related to the synthetic Grand County characteristics and the control groups, with their respective weights. 12 Synthetic Control Methodology 

For the county-level analysis, synthetic control requires specifying the following: 1.  A list of county characteristics potentially relevant to the economic outcome under consideration (shown in Appendix F). 2.  A range of historical years prior to the initiation of timed entry at Arches National Park (2022) over which the analysis assesses the characteristics in Step 1 above. In general, a longer range protects against overfitting while a shorter range protects against including counties that were once, but are no longer, similar to Grand County. Although this report presents results based on a long historical period (1990–2021), the analyses for a shorter or different period yield the same general conclusions as the long-period results. 3.  A list of candidate counties that the synthetic control may include (the analysis determines which of these counties to actually include in the synthetic control and with what weights). This list includes counties with potential similarities to Grand County on observed and, possibly, unobserved characteristics relevant to the economic outcome. The candidate control counties in this analysis include the 34 counties in the Intermountain West that overlap in area with a national park (excluding Grand County). For a complete list of candidate counties, see Appendix F.

Jobs 

The timed-entry system at Arches appears to have generated a positive impact on jobs in Grand County. The estimated effect ranges from 7.0% to 9.4% (about 490–640 jobs annually) for the post-implementation period (2022–2024). The synthetic control model shows a close fit to historical data before 2022, as desired for a good synthetic control. Separation between the actual and counterfactual Grand County jobs represents the difference ascribed to the timed-entry system (Figure 8 and Table 11). 

Total Wages 

Total wages correspond to the wages earned through jobs of the kind discussed above (wage and salary jobs, excluding self-employment). Estimates show a small decline (–2.9%, or –$9 million) in 2022 relative to what would have been expected without timed entry, followed by fairly large increases in 2023 and 2024 (14.3% and 12.0%, or $46 million and $39 million, respectively). Unlike in the case of job counts, here counterfactual total wages are close to (slightly higher than) actual wages in 2021. 

Average Wages 

The timed-entry system at Arches does not appear to have had a large effect on average weekly wages in Grand County. Counterfactual average weekly wages are slightly higher 2022– 2024, although they were higher even before timed entry, in 2021.

# Conclusion 

Synthetic control model results indicate reduced park visitation at Arches attributable to the timed-entry system along with unchanged or somewhat improved economic conditions following timed-entry implementation. Since the estimated differences are not statistically significant, we cannot rule out other potential contributors, independent of timed entry, to improved economic conditions or declines in park visitation. However, numerous robustness checks are consistent with both results—reduced park visitation at Arches and improved economic outcomes in Grand County. For additional details related to robustness modeling exercises, see Appendix F. Results and conclusions related to this analysis do not apply to other parks or similar recreational areas, to other counties, years, or other forms of timed-entry systems. Another limitation involves sample size. With only three years of post-implementation data to analyze, results are vulnerable to events and conditions independent of implementation which may affect visitation or economic outcomes. Additionally, the policy change to implement timed-entry lacks a randomly-assigned policy switch, meaning some factors like increased visitation may predict implementation, potentially leading to an overestimate in the effects of implementation. For additional details related to limitations of the analysis, see Appendix H. The report’s authors suggest various improvements which would strengthen future analytical capabilities. Grand County, NPS, or others could consider additional visitor surveys. Ideally, future researchers could better understand the extent to which visitors—not just visitors to Arches but also visitors to Grand County—view Canyonlands National Park and other park visits as substitute activities or complementary activities to visiting Arches. A better understanding of the composition of county visitors—along with their choice of activities and spending behavior—could help refine estimates presented in this report. Furthermore, the NPS announcement to remove the timed-entry system at Arches during 2026 offers a type of natural experiment and opportunity to collect and measure data, especially related to behavior of park and county visitors. gardner.utah.edu I April 2026 I N F O R M E D D E C I S I O N S TM 15 

Two prior studies looked at the economic effects of the timed-entry reservation system at Arches, one produced by RRC Associates in May 2024 (RRC) and another by Matthew Hancock in April 2025 (Hancock). The two studies largely address different research questions. RRC compares the difference in Arches visitation from 2016–2019 to 2022 (-9.4%) to the corresponding differences for other national parks in the “Intermountain Region.” RRC concludes the decline in Arches visitation is not far enough out of line with visitation growth/ decline in other parks to clearly indicate a negative impact from timed entry. Change in visitation at 18 other national parks ranged from -23.0% to 18.7%, with 5 of 18 parks experiencing lower growth than Arches. Hancock, on the other hand, asked the research question whether visitation patterns in 2022–2024 are statistically different from those before timed entry. This does not necessarily address the question of whether time-entry is responsible for the pattern change. Several recent studies provide more general assessments of national park visitation. Bergstrom et al. (2020) evaluate potential determinants of aggregate U.S. national park visitation, including entrance fees, median personal income, the share of the U.S. population aged 60–84, gasoline prices, the non-white share of the U.S. population, whether after 2001 (post-9/11), U.S. video game industry revenues per player (intended to proxy alternative activities; implemented as revenues divided by total population aged 5–18), and whether 2015–2016 (“Every Kid in a Park” initiative, granting free park admission to 4 th graders and their families), with all monetary values adjusted for inflation. Estimating a linear regression equation, the authors find median personal income, gasoline prices, and the age 60–84 share of U.S. population are statistically significant predictors at the usual 5% level, with visitation being more sensitive to growth rates in the population aged 60-84 than to growth rates in median personal income and gasoline prices. The authors use the estimated regression equation—using all potential determinants of visitation—to forecast annual visitation through 2026. Drugova et al. (2021) evaluate the effects of Utah’s Mighty 5 promotion, an advertising campaign intended to increase visitation to Utah’s five national parks. Using synthetic control methods, the authors estimate the effects of the campaign on each of Utah’s national parks, finding statistically significant effects for three of the five parks (Arches, Canyonlands, and Capitol Reef ). With its similar aims—estimating the causal effect of a policy or other sharp change on national park visitation— this study has served as a helpful guide for the counterfactual park-visitation analysis presented in this report. Two related studies—Jakus and Akhundjanov (2018, 2019)— evaluate the effects of national monument designation on host-county per-capita income. Also using synthetic control methods, the earlier study finds no statistically significant effects from the designation of Grand Staircase–Escalante National Monument on income per-capita in either of two host counties (Grand County, Utah and Kane County, Utah). Using the same basic data and methodology, the more expansive 2019 study considers the potential effects of nine national monuments on 20 host counties (in five states: California, Colorado, Montana, Oregon, and Washington). None of the estimated effects were statistically significant, consistent with national monument designation having small, if any, effects—positive or negative— on local economies (at least as reflected by per-capita income). Like Drugova et al. (2021), these two studies have been helpful references for both data and methodology, particularly for the counterfactual analysis of Grand County economic outcomes.

Accommodation Sector Analysis 

Table C1 shows that following the implementation of the Arches timed-entry system, Grand County’s hotel sector performed reasonably well overall, accommodating much of the room supply increase. Average hotel capacity grew by 18.9% between 2017–2019 and 2022–2024, while occupancy rates declined modestly from 78.9% to 75.1% (−4.7%), indicating that the market absorbed most of the new room supply. At the same time, the average number of hotel rooms occupied increased by 13.2%, reflecting continued growth in overall demand. While nominal average daily rates (ADR) and revenue per available room (RevPAR) rose over this period, inflation-adjusted ADR was flat, and RevPAR declined, suggesting some compression in revenue per room even as total rooms sold increased. Compared to other rural Utah national park gateway counties, including Garfield, Kane, San Juan, Washington, and Wayne, Grand County’s post–timed-entry hotel performance appears generally in line with regional trends rather than being an outlier (Table C2, Figure C1). 12 Occupancy declined across all six counties, with Grand’s 4.7% decrease comparable to Washington (–4.1%) and slightly better than Garfield–San Juan–Wayne (–5.9%) and Kane (–12.3%). 13 Capacity increased across all markets, from 17.5% in Washington to 23.1% in Garfield–San Juan–Wayne. Grand’s 18.9% growth was in the middle, reflecting regional accommodation expansion. In real average daily rate terms, Grand held flat (0.0%), outperforming Garfield–San Juan–Wayne (–6.0%) but trailing Kane (6.0%) and Washington (7.1%). Revenue per available room declined in all peer counties but Washington, where it rose 2.4%, while Grand’s 4.7% drop was moderate compared to the sharper declines in Garfield–San Juan–Wayne (–11.4%) and Kane (–7.0%). Overall, Grand County’s performance trends closely mirror those seen across peer gateway counties, suggesting that post-period lodging dynamics reflect broader regional supply growth and demand normalization rather than effects unique to Grand County. Table C3 indicates that Grand County’s short-term rental market experienced significant growth following implementation of the Arches timed-entry system, though with notable occupancy rate softening. Average short-term rental units expanded 27.4% between 2017–2019 and 2022–2024, reflecting substantial new supply entering the market. At the same time, occupancy rates fell from 64.3% to 56.4% (–12.3%) pre–timed-entry to gardner.utah.edu I April 2026 I N F O R M E D D E C I S I O N S TM 19 

post–timed-entry, a greater decline than in the hotel sector, suggesting demand growth has not fully absorbed the expanded inventory. Unlike hotels, however, short-term rentals achieved real pricing gains. Average daily rates rose 66.8% nominally and 39.0% in real terms, indicating strong growth beyond inflation. As a result, revenue per rental unit increased nominally by 45.2% and in real terms by 21.2%, demonstrating improved revenue productivity despite lower occupancy rates. Overall, the data suggests that while occupancy pressures emerged post–timed-entry, the short-term rental sector expanded rapidly, as did its pricing. Occupancy rates declined in most counties, including Grand (–12.3%), Garfield (–8.6%), Kane (–3.9%), San Juan (–17.5%), and Washington (–5.8%), while Wayne was the lone exception with a 12.5% increase. At the same time, every county experienced substantial short-term rental unit expansion—ranging from 27.4% in Grand to nearly 90.0% in Washington and Wayne—indicating that supply growth has been a widespread regional trend. In terms of pricing power, Grand’s 39.0% real average daily rate growth was the strongest, followed by Washington (29.2%) and Kane (17.3%) and far outperforming Garfield (-4.2%) and San Juan (7.5%). As a result, Grand achieved solid real revenue per rented unit growth (21.2%), comparable to Washington (21.7%) and behind only Wayne (27.8%), while Garfield and San Juan saw revenue per rented unit declines. While some source data are available at higher frequency and date back as far as 1969, datasets constructed for this project use annual frequency and date back to 1990. National park visitation, park budgets, and park geospatial and characteristic data come from the National Park Service. Gasoline prices source from the U.S. Department of Energy while data on cooling degree days (the weather-related control variable) come from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Annual personal income and employment data come from the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), while population and land area estimates source from the U.S. Census Bureau. Labor market indicators, including labor force participation and unemployment rates, come from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS) data library. The analysis draws employment and wage data from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW), providing additional insight into the local labor market. The Utah State Tax Commission represents the source for taxable sales. Additional socioeconomic and community indicators such as educational attainment, disconnected youth rates, premature death rates, subprime credit population, and poverty were accessed from the U.S. Census Bureau via FRED, the U.S. Department of Agriculture, Equifax and Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Urban and rural status and retirement destination data source from the U.S. Office of Management and Budget and the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

This analysis uses synthetic control techniques to estimate the effect of timed-entry on visitation at Arches National Park and economic outcomes in Grand County, Utah. The difference between an actual outcome (e.g., visitation to Arches in 2024) and a counterfactual outcome (reflecting what would have happened in the absence of the policy switch) represents the effect of a policy change. Since actual outcomes are directly observed, the empirical analysis simplifies to estimating the counterfactual outcomes. The synthetic control method estimates counterfactual outcomes as a weighted average of actual outcomes from other units (e.g. parks or counties) which operate without a timed-entry system. The weights—which are constrained to be non-negative and summing to one—are determined such that the aggregate or “synthetic” park or county closely matches the characteristics (e.g., historical unemployment rates) of Arches or Grand County in the years prior to timed-entry, at least for those characteristics that are the strongest predictors of historical outcomes. The constraint on weights prevents extrapolation, ensuring the synthetic control exists within the bounds of observed park or county outcomes. As with units, the analysis weights characteristics, with non-negative weights constrained to sum to one. Whereas unit weights reflect the closest weighted average of no-policy-switch units to the treated unit, characteristic weights essentially define “closeness” between two sets of attribute values—differences in characteristic values do not have to “count” the same for each characteristic. Analysts determine characteristic weights using the most common approach, choosing weights that yield the closest fit, based on the mean squared prediction error (MSPE) between actual historical outcomes and synthetic historical outcomes. 14 A synthetic Arches or Grand County that does not resemble its real-life counterpart, pre-switch, is unlikely to provide a credible estimate of counterfactual outcomes post-switch. Therefore, an important part of assessing estimated effects— the difference between actual and counterfactual outcomes— is assessing the degree to which important park- and county-level characteristics matched each other by the synthetic control, including how closely the synthetic control reproduces the level of visitation and economic outcomes experienced at Arches and in Grand County. The synthetic control must do more than closely resemble its actual counterpart on observable characteristics. A recommended practice is to pre-select a pool of potential control parks or counties (those parks or counties without timed-entry systems) that seem likely to have similar unobserved determinants of outcomes to the affected park or county. 15 To that end, the county-level analysis bases on 34 national park counties (not counting Grand County, Utah) in the Intermountain West, where a “national park county” is a county that shares area with a national park. This only includes counties that do not host a national park with a broad-based timed-entry system similar in scope to Arches’ (Table 8). Such counties likely have persistent features in common beyond measurable data in this study. National parks (or their host counties) without timed-entry but that were likely affected by timed-entry at Arches should be excluded from the list of potential control parks (likewise for counties). Since affected parks have higher or lower visitation than they would have without timed-entry at Arches, the difference between actual Arches and a synthetic control comprised of affected parks may systematically under- or over-state the estimated effect of the policy switch on Arches. For example, if implementation of timed-entry at Arches shifted visitation to Utah’s other national parks, then post-implementation visitation trends in those parks (or a combination involving those parks) will be larger than it would have been absent timed-entry at Arches, leading, in this example, to a systematic over-estimation of the effect on visitation at Arches. The national parks that best resemble Arches in the pre-implementation years may also be those most affected by policy changes at Arches. The main model results retain all national parks—except those with broad timed-entry systems— including national parks in Utah that plausibly experienced increased or decreased visitation on account of timed-entry at Arches. Similarly, the main county-level analyses include all national park counties—except those hosting national parks with broad timed-entry systems. Robustness checks explore sensitivities to these assumptions, as explained in Appendix F. The report’s main cases base off the level of visitation or economic outcomes, instead of growth or growth rates in these outcomes. Since growth or growth rates tend to be more volatile than levels they tend to increase the risk of overfitting—creating a synthetic control that accidentally resembles Arches or Grand County pre-implementation but loses this resemblance post-implementation. 16 On the other hand, some county outcomes (e.g., total jobs) vary quite a bit in level from one county to the next, which can complicate the creation of a close-fitting synthetic control. Other outcomes, such as average wages, per capita income, and the unemployment rate do not have such large level differences. As with the list of potential control parks or counties, and whether to exclude potentially affected parks or counties, Appendix F contains sensitivities of robustness results testing whether to model outcomes in levels or growth rates.

Economic and Fiscal Impacts 

The counterfactual analysis provides annual “lost” Arches National Park visits in 2022, 2023 and 2024, calculated as the difference between estimated visits in the counterfactual scenario and the actual number of visits. Using data from a 2022 survey of Arches visitors, Gardner Institute analysts divide the number of lost visits by 1.41, the average number of visits to the park by each visitor. This gives the number of lost visitors. The 2022 survey also provides average spending per person per day and average length of stay. Multiplying lost visitors by average spending per person per day and by average length of stay yields an upper bound of total lost spending. The analysis also examined total actual visitor spending in Grand County in 2017 through 2019 and 2022 through 2024. Dividing by the actual number of park visits gives average spending per Arches National Park visit. While this does not represent actual spending by park visitors, it does reveal average, inflation-adjusted spending 25.8% lower before implementation of the timed-entry system (2017–2019) than after (2022–2024). Assuming the lost visitors would have spent at the pre–timed-entry rate provides a lower bound of total foregone visitor spending. The analysis assumes all foregone visitor spending would have happened in Grand County. Given that 97% of 2022 Arches National Park survey respondents visited Moab, 17% visited Green River, and less than 10% visited any community in San Juan County, Arches visitors likely made most of their expenditures in Grand, although a small portion may have occurred in Emery, San Juan, and/or elsewhere. Next, the statistical significance of an estimated difference refers to the likelihood that such a result comes by chance alone. In the context of synthetic control, placebo tests assess the statistical significance of an estimated effect. In the most common variant of placebo testing, used in this analysis, the analysis compares the effect of the policy switch on the unit subject to the switch (e.g. Arches or Grand County) to the effects estimated on units that were not actually subject to the switch (other parks and counties). If statistically significant, the estimated effect at the treated unit stands out against the estimated effects at untreated units. The test compares the ratio of the post-treatment MSPE to the pre-treatment MSPE for the treated unit to the corresponding ratios for untreated units, using each unit’s synthetic control as the predictor of its pre-and post- treatment outcomes. Synthetic controls of untreated units should predict post-treatment outcomes about as accurately as pre-treatment outcomes. To the extent the policy change affects the treated unit, its synthetic control should predict outcomes less accurately in the post-treatment period. A p-value measures the statistical significance of an estimated difference. In this context, the p-value equates to the percentile of the treated unit’s post-/pre-MSPE ratio among the corresponding ratios of all units. A statistically significant difference at the 5% level of significance (a traditional and standard threshold in statistics, used in this report) means no more than 5% of units have ratios as extreme as the treated unit. If the treated unit’s ratio falls solidly within the range of the untreated ratios, then the placebo test concludes that the difference is not statistically significant. Note that the magnitude required to exceed the threshold for “typical”—and so be deemed “statistically significant”—will vary by case and even differences seemingly large in a practical sense may not be large enough relative to background data variation to be statistically significant. Also, statistical significance does not imply that treatment caused the difference. 

Visitor Spending Analysis 

In this analysis, “visitor spending” includes expenditures on accommodations, auto repair, car rentals, gasoline, grocery stores, restaurants, retail, and other personal services by visitors traveling at least 50 miles (one way) to Grand County. It includes leisure and business spending by in-state and out-of-state domestic travelers, as well as international visitors. Visitor spending estimates derive from taxable sales and sales tax revenue data from the Utah State Tax Commission and visitor market share data from Visa Destination Insights. The analysis utilizes Visa data to estimate the visitor share of spending by market segment. As visitor spending flows through the local economy, it generates impacts beyond the initial “direct” amounts spent at hotels, restaurants, retail shops and other establishments. The businesses at which visitors spend their money use those dollars to pay their employees and purchase goods and services from other local businesses, who in turn do the same. These constitute “indirect” effects. The employees of the direct and indirect businesses spend a portion of their earnings in the local economy as well, generating “induced” effects. These additional rounds of indirect and induced spending, combined with the initial visitor spending, represent the total visitor spending impact. The Gardner Institute used the IMPLAN model to generate the indirect and induced effects. Fiscal impacts represent a combination of direct sales taxes calculated by the Gardner Institute and direct, indirect and induced taxes calculated by the IMPLAN model. The Gardner Institute multiplies estimated visitor expenditures by the specific state and local sales tax rates appropriate for each spending category. Analysts then add IMPLAN’s indirect and induced sales tax revenues to these amounts. Additional County-Level Economic Analysis Details 

This section provides further details on the county-level economic outcome analyses summarized in the body of the report. Tables illustrate the synthetic control methodology’s resulting characteristic and county weights. 

Jobs 

The timed-entry system at Arches appears to have contributed to a positive impact on jobs in Grand County. The estimated effect ranges from 7.0% to 9.4% (about 490–640 jobs annually) for the post-implementation period (2022–2024). For total jobs, the best-fitting synthetic Grand County combines Kane County, Utah (68.0%), Park County, Montana (17.0%), Eddy County, New Mexico (9.4%), Washington County, Utah (5.3%), and Flathead County, Montana (0.2%). This synthetic control more closely resembles actual Grand County than does the average national park county. Additionally, the synthetic control shows a close fit to historical data before 2022, as desired for a good synthetic control. 

Total Wages 

The best fitting synthetic Grand County for total wages combines Garfield County, Utah (39.8%), Kane County, Utah (37.1%), Gallatin County, Montana (14.7%), and Teton County, Wyoming (8.3%). The synthetic Grand County resembles actual Grand County closely in pre-implementation characteristics. Unlike the case of job counts, here counterfactual total wages are close (slightly higher) to actual wages in 2021. Note that total wage growth can be volatile: Garfield County, the largest contributor to synthetic Grand County, experienced the largest decline in total wages over 2021–2024 (about -20%), while another contributor to synthetic Grand County, Gallatin County, experienced one of the largest increases (almost 20%).

gardner.utah.edu I April 2026 I N F O R M E D D E C I S I O N S TM 1Analysis in Brief 

Grand County, Utah experienced positive economic impacts and growth in average annual visitor-generated tax revenue after implementation of a timed-entry reservation system at Arches National Park (Arches) in 2022. 

Visitation 

While visitation to Arches remained relatively flat between 2022 and 2024 (0.4% increase), statistical analysis indicates that the timed-entry system likely reduced Arches visitation relative to a counterfactual Arches baseline with no timed-entry system. 

Visitor Spending 

Had no other changes occurred, the visitation reduction would likely have led to foregone visitor spending in the years since implementation (2022–2024). However, potential foregone visitor spending from the timed-entry system appears more than offset by higher spending within Grand County from business travelers and visitors to Arches and other nearby national and state parks, and from those drawn to Grand County’s beautiful landscapes and diverse recreational opportunities outside of those parks. 

Economy 

Since 2022, Grand County’s economy experienced positive growth, as measured by jobs, total wages, and other standard economic indicators. A range of factors beyond timed entry also influenced Grand County's economy, making timed entry's effect more uncertain. 

Key Findings • Grand County’s Visitor Economy – Tourism jobs in Grand County increased 16.3% post–timed-entry (2022–2024 average), relative to pre–timed-entry (2017–2019 average). Adjusting for inflation, visitor spending and visitor-generated tax revenue increased 22.2% and 27.8% respectively. However, both visitor spending and visitor-generated tax revenue declined slightly between 2022 and 2024. 

• Arches Timed-Entry System – The timed-entry system reduced Arches visitation by an estimated 170,000 people (14.1% reduction from estimated counterfactual totals) on average per year between 2022 and 2024. 

• Foregone Visitor Spending and Local Fiscal Impacts – 

Had no other changes occurred, reduced visitation would have led to between $41.4 and $55.1 million of foregone annual visitor spending (9% to 11% reduction from estimated counterfactual totals) in Grand County. Local net fiscal impacts (revenues less expenditures) associated with this foregone spending range from negative $1.9–$2.6 million in 2022 to negative $2.0–$2.7 million in 2024, meaning estimated lost tax revenue exceeds cost savings. 

• Grand County’s Positive Economic Outcomes – 

A combination of factors since implementation of the timed-entry system at Arches—including a possible change in the composition of visitors to Arches, increased visitors at Canyonlands National Park and Dead Horse Point State Park, and the availability of other recreational and business activities in the county—also influenced Grand County's economy, making timed entry's effect on broader economic outcomes more uncertain.

# Introduction 

In 2022, the National Park Service implemented a timed-entry reservation system at Arches National Park (Arches) in Grand County, Utah. This analysis explores Grand County’s economic and visitation impacts since then. While visitation to Arches remained relatively flat between 2022 and 2024 (0.4% increase), statistical analysis indicates that the timed-entry system likely reduced Arches visitation relative to a counterfactual baseline with no timed-entry system. The visitation reduction would have led to foregone visitor spending estimated between $41.4 million and $55.1 million annually in the years since implementation (2022–2024), all else equal. However, potential foregone visitor spending from the timed-entry system appears more than offset by higher actual spending within Grand County from business travelers and visitors to Arches and other nearby national and state parks, and from those drawn to Grand County’s stunning landscapes and diverse recreational opportunities outside of those parks. Grand County is home to two of Utah’s five national parks—Arches and a portion of Canyonlands—as well as two state parks—Utahraptor and a portion of Dead Horse Point (Figure 1). Since 2022, Grand County’s economy experienced positive growth, as measured by jobs, total wages, and other economic indicators. While varying by economic indicator, a range of analytical approaches signals positive economic impacts countywide, relative to a counterfactual Grand County that assumes no timed entry at Arches. The pre–timed-entry system analysis for this report includes years 2017 to 2019, omitting 2020 and 2021 because of anomalous conditions during that time related to the COVID-19 pandemic. The post–timed-entry system analysis focuses on years 2022 through 2024. While visitation data and some economic data for 2025 are now available at the time of publication, these data were not available during the project’s research phase. Also of note, 2025 presents a unique data year due to the federal government shutdown during October and November, which reduced staffing at Arches and eliminated the timed-entry system earlier than normal.

# Timed-Entry Background 

Since 2017, seven U.S. national parks (including Arches) and one national monument introduced timed-entry or vehicle reservation systems to manage congestion, enhance visitor experiences, and protect natural resources (Table 1). Haleakalā National Park in Hawaii first implemented a reservation system (2017) to manage visitor traffic entering the park during early morning hours for sunrise viewing. Other parks soon followed: Muir Woods National Monument launched a permanent parking and shuttle reservation system in 2018; Acadia National Park (2020) piloted a reservation requirement for Cadillac Summit Road, which the park permanently implemented in 2021; and Rocky Mountain National Park piloted a timed-entry reservation system in 2020 (following four years of testing a first-come/first-served park entry system). That same year (2020), Yosemite National Park tested multiple timed-entry systems and has since maintained limited entry reservations during peak seasons, weekends, and holidays. In 2024, Glacier and Mount Rainier National Parks launched timed-entry pilots, which they maintained with some adjustments in 2025. Arches National Park piloted a timed-entry system from April to October from 2022 to 2024, adjusting it in 2025 with staggered dates and limited entry hours. In early 2026, the National Park Service announced it would not use the timed-entry system at Arches in 2026. 1 Previous studies explore the Arches timed-entry system and its effects while other related literature provide context to Arches and park visitation generally. See Appendix A for additional details. Across all parks, the design of timed-entry and vehicle registration systems controls visitation during high-use periods, requires small non-refundable processing fees, and relies on advance, online reservations. Most systems open bookings months in advance, with limited release closer to entry. 2 Timed-entry windows regulate arrival periods but generally allow visitors to stay once inside, and early-morning or late-evening entry (outside of reservation hours) remains unrestricted in most cases. While national park reservation systems share objectives, they vary in scope, seasonality, and complexity. 3Reservation coverage also differs by park, from regulating access to specific roads or corridors to covering full-park entry. 4Park administrative models and fees also range widely. 5 Overall, U.S. national park reservation systems reflect the National Park Service’s evolving strategy to balance access and preservation through adaptive visitor management. 6

Following implementation of the Arches timed-entry system, Grand County’s visitor economy expanded overall, though with mixed accommodation performance. Average hotel capacity grew by 18.9% between 2017–2019 and 2022–2024, while occupancy rates declined modestly from 78.9% to 75.1%, indicating the market absorbed most of the new room supply. Additionally, the average number of hotel rooms occupied increased by 13.2%, reflecting continued demand growth. While nominal average daily rates (ADR) and revenue per available room (RevPAR) rose over this period, inflation-adjusted ADR was flat, and RevPAR declined, suggesting some compression in revenue per room. These accommodation trends are consistent with broader regional patterns among Utah’s rural national park gateway counties. In contrast, the short-term rental sector expanded more rapidly and achieved occupied room night and pricing gains despite lower occupancy rates. This highlights nightly rate growth along with inventory expansion. For additional details related to Grand County’s accommodation sector, see Appendix C. Beyond lodging, visitor spending and related tax revenues both increased in real (inflation-adjusted) terms, and total private-sec-tor, public-sector and tourism employment grew (Table 3). Taken together, the data indicate positive visitor economy outcomes in Grand County post–timed-entry, marked by supply growth and continued expansion in overall visitor economic activity.

Visitor-Generated Tax Revenue 

State and local tax revenues generated by visitor spending in Grand County increased overall in the post–timed-entry period compared to the pre–timed-entry period, despite year-over declines in 2023 and 2024 (Table 4). While the previous sections illustrate trends in visitation, visitor spending, and other indicators, those analyses do not equate correlation to causation. In this section and the following section, the statistical analysis seeks to quantify the causal effect, if any, of timed-entry at Arches on subsequent visitation. The park-level statistical analysis estimates the visitation that Arches would have experienced without timed entry beginning in 2022. The authors estimate this counterfactual outcome using an empirical technique called synthetic control. This analysis approximates, as closely as possible, a “parallel” or “counterfactual” version of Arches, similar in all relevant ways to the actual Arches National Park but without timed entry. The difference in visitation between the actual and parallel versions of Arches approximates the effects of timed entry. Synthetic control estimates Arches visitation without timed entry as a weighted average of the visitation of other national parks that were similar to Arches prior to 2022 but that do not have timed-entry systems. For a complete list of candidate parks, see Appendix F. The synthetic control algorithm assigns weights to candidate parks, where those with non-zero weights become "control" parks. Since control parks closely predict Arches visitation before timed entry (with actual Arches visitation nearly identical to counterfactual Arches), then they should continue to closely predict counterfactual Arches after timed-entry implementation at Arches. The model specification controls for various potential explanatory factors of visitation, such as gasoline prices, weather, the population of the nearest population center, and other factors to isolate the effect of timed entry. This park-level analysis follows—in method and various implementation details—a recent study of the effects of the Mighty 5 ad campaign on visitation at Utah’s national parks. 8 Appendix E provides further details on the methodology of synthetic control. The timed-entry system at Arches National Park decreased park visitation, with estimated declines of 13.7% (200,000 visits) in 2022, 16.5% (244,000 visits) in 2023, and 19.0% (279,000 visits) in 2024. This analysis divides the number of lost visits by 1.41, the average number of visits to the park by each visitor, to yield the number of lost visitors. 9Table 7 shows the differences in visitation between Arches and counterfactual Arches for 2022 to 2024. In addition to these estimated differences, the uncertainty range (middle 50%) reflects a range of estimates based on the interquartile range of estimates from 30 model variations. Appendix F discusses these model variations.

Statistical Definitions Synthetic control – Synthetic control represents a weighted average of characteristics from other, non-treated units, forming a hypothetical unit for comparison. In this report, other units consist of other parks and counties (not Arches or Grand County). Synthetic controls estimate counterfactual visitation at Arches and counterfactual economic outcomes in Grand County, had timed-entry not been implemented in 2022. To simplify terminology, this report uses the term “counterfactual” to refer to either a synthetic control or an estimated counterfactual outcome. 

Statistical significance – A statistically significant difference in measured outcomes is one large enough to confidently say it reflects a true difference in the underlying unmeasurable outcomes; a difference that is not statistically significant is too small to detect with confidence, given random variation in observable data. 

Interquartile or uncertainty range – The interquartile range refers to the middle 50% of data, meaning data points falling between the 25 th and 75 th percentiles. This does not represent a confidence interval. Here, the shaded region in Figure 7 represents the interquartile range of 30 different estimates for estimating counterfactual visits at Arches from 30 unique model specifications. An estimate may fall outside the range, meaning the estimate was somewhat less typical (less than the 25th percentile or greater than the 75th percentile of all estimates). Results tables 7 and 11 through 14 refer to the interquartile range as the uncertainty range. For additional details, see Appendix F.

Data and Sources 

This analysis relies on two datasets, built from acombination of federal and state data, as well as other public sources, to conduct statistical modeling of the economic impacts resulting from the implementation of the timed-entry system at Arches National Park. The first dataset contains park-level data for all national parks in the U.S. The second dataset contains county-level data for Grand County, and all other counties in the U.S. with a national park. Where possible, data begins in 1990 and continues at annual frequency until the most recent year of available data. The park-level dataset contains park characteristics such as size, timed-entry status, budget, number of entrances, and capacity, as well as other control variables that could explain visitation data changes such as price of gasoline, a weather-related variable, and other data. Visitation counts represent outcome data for the first set of statistical models. The county-level dataset contains county characteristics such as size, population, percentage of adult population with a college degree, urban/rural status, etc., as well as economic data related to income and wages, employment and unemployment, taxable sales, and other indicators. Six of the economic variables serve as outcome variables in the statistical modeling. Appendix D summarizes all data (Tables D1 and D2), along with details of their geographic coverage, time-period coverage, and available frequency.

The forgone annual park visits estimated previously in this section could represent lost visitor spending in and around Arches National Park. The Gardner Institute estimates that, all else equal, forgone visitor spending could range from $34.4– $45.9 million in 2022 to $47.7–$63.5 million in 2024 (in inflation-adjusted 2025 dollars) (Table 10). The statistical analysis does not align with observed data trends because the “all else equal” assumption does not completely hold true. For example, rather than maintaining an identical visitor profile as the “all else equal” assumption holds, the timed-entry system could have changed the composition of visitors in reality, with fewer casual day-trippers and more intentional visitors who plan well in advance and might spend more time and money in Grand County. Further research should explore these potential visitor profile changes. See the Conclusion for author recommendations. Holding other assumptions in the economy constant (ceteris paribus conditions)—such as visitor profile, visitor behavior, ignoring substitution effects, etc.—results in negative economic and fiscal impacts. See Appendix G for the ceteris paribus analysis. A credible synthetic control for visitation at Arches should closely resemble Arches prior to the beginning of the timed-entry system (2022). Table 9 shows annual visitation for Arches, average annual visitation in the full sample of national parks without timed-entry (“All-Park Average”), and the annual visitation for synthetic (counterfactual) Arches. In general, characteristics of synthetic Arches more closely match actual pre–timed-entry Arches than does the full sample of national parks. For example, annual visitation from 1990–1997 averages 776,848 for Arches, 613,540 (27% lower than actual) for the full sample of national parks, and 842,391 for the synthetic control (8% above actual). Visitation in the other three historical periods follows similar patterns. Only one case—gasoline prices—shows the full-sample average closer than the synthetic control but the difference is small and gas prices receive only a very small weight (i.e., they were not very useful for predicting historical visitation 1990–2021 above and beyond the other variables). The best-fitting synthetic control for park visitation consists of Canyonlands (36.2%), Zion (24.0%), Joshua Tree (18.6%), Bryce Canyon (11.4%), Theodore Roosevelt National Park (4.9%), Wrangell–St. Elias National Park (2.9%), Yellowstone (1.2%), and a few others with weights less than 1% (Table 8). 

# County-Level Economic Analysis 

The county-level statistical analysis estimates the economic outcomes Grand County would have experienced without the initiation of the Arches timed-entry system in 2022. As in the park visitation analysis, the authors employ synthetic control modeling to estimate these counterfactual outcomes. This widely deployed method provided the basis for two studies on the effects of national monument designations on host county per capita income—including analyses of Utah’s Garfield and Kane counties. These studies serve as helpful guides for the analysis of Grand County. 10,11 This analysis approximates, as closely as possible, a “parallel” or “counterfactual” version of Grand County, identical in all relevant ways to actual Grand County but without timed entry at Arches National Park. The difference in economic outcomes between the actual and parallel versions of Grand County approximates the effects of timed entry on those outcomes. Synthetic control estimates Grand County outcomes without timed entry as a weighted average of the outcomes of other counties that were similar to Grand County prior to 2022 but that do not host national parks with timed-entry systems. Since control counties closely predict Grand County economic outcomes before timed entry (when actual Grand County is nearly identical to counterfactual Grand County), they should continue to closely predict counterfactual Grand County after timed entry at Arches. The model specification controls for various potential explanatory factors of economic outcomes, such as educational attainment, urban/rural status, population, and other county factors to isolate the effect of timed entry. To the extent the Arches timed-entry system reduced visitation and to the extent people instead visited other parks in Grand County, or other county attractions, the county-level analysis captures those effects. Known as “substitution effects,” one activity substitutes for another based on individual preferences and choices. However, the county-level analysis cannot control for every known event that could have increased economic outcomes after implementation of the timed-entry system. 

Model Results 

The analysis assessed the impact of timed entry on six economic outcomes: job counts, total wages, average wages, total income, income per capita, and the unemployment rate. Appendix F contains results for total income and income per capita, along with additional details for each economic outcome related to the synthetic Grand County characteristics and the control groups, with their respective weights. For the county-level analysis, synthetic control requires specifying the following: 1.  A list of county characteristics potentially relevant to the economic outcome under consideration (shown in Appendix F). 2.  A range of historical years prior to the initiation of timed entry at Arches National Park (2022) over which the analysis assesses the characteristics in Step 1 above. In general, a longer range protects against overfitting while a shorter range protects against including counties that were once, but are no longer, similar to Grand County. Although this report presents results based on a long historical period (1990–2021), the analyses for a shorter or different period yield the same general conclusions as the long-period results. 3.  A list of candidate counties that the synthetic control may include (the analysis determines which of these counties to actually include in the synthetic control and with what weights). This list includes counties with potential similarities to Grand County on observed and, possibly, unobserved characteristics relevant to the economic outcome. The candidate control counties in this analysis include the 34 counties in the Intermountain West that overlap in area with a national park (excluding Grand County). Jobs 

The timed-entry system at Arches appears to have generated a positive impact on jobs in Grand County. The estimated effect ranges from 7.0% to 9.4% (about 490–640 jobs annually) for the post-implementation period (2022–2024). Total Wages 

Total wages correspond to the wages earned through jobs of the kind discussed above (wage and salary jobs, excluding self-employment). Average Wages
