# Conclusion 

Synthetic control model results indicate reduced park visitation at Arches attributable to the timed-entry system along with unchanged or somewhat improved economic conditions following timed-entry implementation. Since the estimated differences are not statistically significant, we cannot rule out other potential contributors, independent of timed entry, to improved economic conditions or declines in park visitation. However, numerous robustness checks are consistent with both results—reduced park visitation at Arches and improved economic outcomes in Grand County. For additional details related to robustness modeling exercises, see Appendix F. Results and conclusions related to this analysis do not apply to other parks or similar recreational areas, to other counties, years, or other forms of timed-entry systems. Another limitation involves sample size. With only three years of post-implementation data to analyze, results are vulnerable to events and conditions independent of implementation which may affect visitation or economic outcomes. Additionally, the policy change to implement timed-entry lacks a randomly-assigned policy switch, meaning some factors like increased visitation may predict implementation, potentially leading to an overestimate in the effects of implementation. For additional details related to limitations of the analysis, see Appendix H. The report’s authors suggest various improvements which would strengthen future analytical capabilities. Grand County, NPS, or others could consider additional visitor surveys. Ideally, future researchers could better understand the extent to which visitors—not just visitors to Arches but also visitors to Grand County—view Canyonlands National Park and other park visits as substitute activities or complementary activities to visiting Arches. A better understanding of the composition of county visitors—along with their choice of activities and spending behavior—could help refine estimates presented in this report. Furthermore, the NPS announcement to remove the timed-entry system at Arches during 2026 offers a type of natural experiment and opportunity to collect and measure data, especially related to behavior of park and county visitors. gardner.utah.edu I April 2026 I N F O R M E D D E C I S I O N S TM 15 

Two prior studies looked at the economic effects of the timed-entry reservation system at Arches, one produced by RRC Associates in May 2024 (RRC) and another by Matthew Hancock in April 2025 (Hancock). The two studies largely address different research questions. RRC compares the difference in Arches visitation from 2016–2019 to 2022 (-9.4%) to the corresponding differences for other national parks in the “Intermountain Region.” RRC concludes the decline in Arches visitation is not far enough out of line with visitation growth/ decline in other parks to clearly indicate a negative impact from timed entry. Change in visitation at 18 other national parks ranged from -23.0% to 18.7%, with 5 of 18 parks experiencing lower growth than Arches. Hancock, on the other hand, asked the research question whether visitation patterns in 2022–2024 are statistically different from those before timed entry. This does not necessarily address the question of whether time-entry is responsible for the pattern change. Several recent studies provide more general assessments of national park visitation. Bergstrom et al. (2020) evaluate potential determinants of aggregate U.S. national park visitation, including entrance fees, median personal income, the share of the U.S. population aged 60–84, gasoline prices, the non-white share of the U.S. population, whether after 2001 (post-9/11), U.S. video game industry revenues per player (intended to proxy alternative activities; implemented as revenues divided by total population aged 5–18), and whether 2015–2016 (“Every Kid in a Park” initiative, granting free park admission to 4 th graders and their families), with all monetary values adjusted for inflation. Estimating a linear regression equation, the authors find median personal income, gasoline prices, and the age 60–84 share of U.S. population are statistically significant predictors at the usual 5% level, with visitation being more sensitive to growth rates in the population aged 60-84 than to growth rates in median personal income and gasoline prices. The authors use the estimated regression equation—using all potential determinants of visitation—to forecast annual visitation through 2026. Drugova et al. (2021) evaluate the effects of Utah’s Mighty 5 promotion, an advertising campaign intended to increase visitation to Utah’s five national parks. Using synthetic control methods, the authors estimate the effects of the campaign on each of Utah’s national parks, finding statistically significant effects for three of the five parks (Arches, Canyonlands, and Capitol Reef ). With its similar aims—estimating the causal effect of a policy or other sharp change on national park visitation— this study has served as a helpful guide for the counterfactual park-visitation analysis presented in this report. Two related studies—Jakus and Akhundjanov (2018, 2019)— evaluate the effects of national monument designation on host-county per-capita income. Also using synthetic control methods, the earlier study finds no statistically significant effects from the designation of Grand Staircase–Escalante National Monument on income per-capita in either of two host counties (Grand County, Utah and Kane County, Utah). Using the same basic data and methodology, the more expansive 2019 study considers the potential effects of nine national monuments on 20 host counties (in five states: California, Colorado, Montana, Oregon, and Washington). None of the estimated effects were statistically significant, consistent with national monument designation having small, if any, effects—positive or negative— on local economies (at least as reflected by per-capita income). Like Drugova et al. (2021), these two studies have been helpful references for both data and methodology, particularly for the counterfactual analysis of Grand County economic outcomes.

Accommodation Sector Analysis 

Table C1 shows that following the implementation of the Arches timed-entry system, Grand County’s hotel sector performed reasonably well overall, accommodating much of the room supply increase. Average hotel capacity grew by 18.9% between 2017–2019 and 2022–2024, while occupancy rates declined modestly from 78.9% to 75.1% (−4.7%), indicating that the market absorbed most of the new room supply. At the same time, the average number of hotel rooms occupied increased by 13.2%, reflecting continued growth in overall demand. While nominal average daily rates (ADR) and revenue per available room (RevPAR) rose over this period, inflation-adjusted ADR was flat, and RevPAR declined, suggesting some compression in revenue per room even as total rooms sold increased. Compared to other rural Utah national park gateway counties, including Garfield, Kane, San Juan, Washington, and Wayne, Grand County’s post–timed-entry hotel performance appears generally in line with regional trends rather than being an outlier (Table C2, Figure C1). 12 Occupancy declined across all six counties, with Grand’s 4.7% decrease comparable to Washington (–4.1%) and slightly better than Garfield–San Juan–Wayne (–5.9%) and Kane (–12.3%). 13 Capacity increased across all markets, from 17.5% in Washington to 23.1% in Garfield–San Juan–Wayne. Grand’s 18.9% growth was in the middle, reflecting regional accommodation expansion. In real average daily rate terms, Grand held flat (0.0%), outperforming Garfield–San Juan–Wayne (–6.0%) but trailing Kane (6.0%) and Washington (7.1%). Revenue per available room declined in all peer counties but Washington, where it rose 2.4%, while Grand’s 4.7% drop was moderate compared to the sharper declines in Garfield–San Juan–Wayne (–11.4%) and Kane (–7.0%). Overall, Grand County’s performance trends closely mirror those seen across peer gateway counties, suggesting that post-period lodging dynamics reflect broader regional supply growth and demand normalization rather than effects unique to Grand County. Average short-term rental units expanded 27.4% between 2017–2019 and 2022–2024, reflecting substantial new supply entering the market. This analysis uses synthetic control techniques to estimate the effect of timed-entry on visitation at Arches National Park and economic outcomes in Grand County, Utah. The difference between an actual outcome (e.g., visitation to Arches in 2024) and a counterfactual outcome (reflecting what would have happened in the absence of the policy switch) represents the effect of a policy change. Since actual outcomes are directly observed, the empirical analysis simplifies to estimating the counterfactual outcomes. The synthetic control method estimates counterfactual outcomes as a weighted average of actual outcomes from other units (e.g. parks or counties) which operate without a timed-entry system. The weights—which are constrained to be non-negative and summing to one—are determined such that the aggregate or “synthetic” park or county closely matches the characteristics (e.g., historical unemployment rates) of Arches or Grand County in the years prior to timed-entry, at least for those characteristics that are the strongest predictors of historical outcomes. The constraint on weights prevents extrapolation, ensuring the synthetic control exists within the bounds of observed park or county outcomes. As with units, the analysis weights characteristics, with non-negative weights constrained to sum to one. Whereas unit weights reflect the closest weighted average of no-policy-switch units to the treated unit, characteristic weights essentially define “closeness” between two sets of attribute values—differences in characteristic values do not have to “count” the same for each characteristic. Analysts determine characteristic weights using the most common approach, choosing weights that yield the closest fit, based on the mean squared prediction error (MSPE) between actual historical outcomes and synthetic historical outcomes. 14 A synthetic Arches or Grand County that does not resemble its real-life counterpart, pre-switch, is unlikely to provide a credible estimate of counterfactual outcomes post-switch. Therefore, an important part of assessing estimated effects— the difference between actual and counterfactual outcomes— is assessing the degree to which important park- and county-level characteristics matched each other by the synthetic control, including how closely the synthetic control reproduces the level of visitation and economic outcomes experienced at Arches and in Grand County. The synthetic control must do more than closely resemble its actual counterpart on observable characteristics. A recommended practice is to pre-select a pool of potential control parks or counties (those parks or counties without timed-entry systems) that seem likely to have similar unobserved determinants of outcomes to the affected park or county. 15 To that end, the county-level analysis bases on 34 national park counties (not counting Grand County, Utah) in the Intermountain West, where a “national park county” is a county that shares area with a national park. This only includes counties that do not host a national park with a broad-based timed-entry system similar in scope to Arches’ (Table 8). Such counties likely have persistent features in common beyond measurable data in this study. National parks (or their host counties) without timed-entry but that were likely affected by timed-entry at Arches should be excluded from the list of potential control parks (likewise for counties). Since affected parks have higher or lower visitation than they would have without timed-entry at Arches, the difference between actual Arches and a synthetic control comprised of affected parks may systematically under- or over-state the estimated effect of the policy switch on Arches. For example, if implementation of timed-entry at Arches shifted visitation to Utah’s other national parks, then post-implementation visitation trends in those parks (or a combination involving those parks) will be larger than it would have been absent timed-entry at Arches, leading, in this example, to a systematic over-estimation of the effect on visitation at Arches. The national parks that best resemble Arches in the pre-implementation years may also be those most affected by policy changes at Arches. The main model results retain all national parks—except those with broad timed-entry systems— including national parks in Utah that plausibly experienced increased or decreased visitation on account of timed-entry at Arches. Similarly, the main county-level analyses include all national park counties—except those hosting national parks with broad timed-entry systems. Robustness checks explore sensitivities to these assumptions, as explained in Appendix F. The report’s main cases base off the level of visitation or economic outcomes, instead of growth or growth rates in these outcomes. Since growth or growth rates tend to be more volatile than levels they tend to increase the risk of overfitting—creating a synthetic control that accidentally resembles Arches or Grand County pre-implementation but loses this resemblance post-implementation. 16 On the other hand, some county outcomes (e.g., total jobs) vary quite a bit in level from one county to the next, which can complicate the creation of a close-fitting synthetic control. Other outcomes, such as average wages, per capita income, and the unemployment rate do not have such large level differences. As with the list of potential control parks or counties, and whether to exclude potentially affected parks or counties, Appendix F contains sensitivities of robustness results testing whether to model outcomes in levels or growth rates.

Economic and Fiscal Impacts 

The counterfactual analysis provides annual “lost” Arches National Park visits in 2022, 2023 and 2024, calculated as the difference between estimated visits in the counterfactual scenario and the actual number of visits. Using data from a 2022 survey of Arches visitors, Gardner Institute analysts divide the number of lost visits by 1.41, the average number of visits to the park by each visitor. This gives the number of lost visitors. The 2022 survey also provides average spending per person per day and average length of stay. Multiplying lost visitors by average spending per person per day and by average length of stay yields an upper bound of total lost spending. The analysis also examined total actual visitor spending in Grand County in 2017 through 2019 and 2022 through 2024. Dividing by the actual number of park visits gives average spending per Arches National Park visit. While this does not represent actual spending by park visitors, it does reveal average, inflation-adjusted spending 25.8% lower before implementation of the timed-entry system (2017–2019) than after (2022–2024). Assuming the lost visitors would have spent at the pre–timed-entry rate provides a lower bound of total foregone visitor spending. The analysis assumes all foregone visitor spending would have happened in Grand County. Given that 97% of 2022 Arches National Park survey respondents visited Moab, 17% visited Green River, and less than 10% visited any community in San Juan County, Arches visitors likely made most of their expenditures in Grand, although a small portion may have occurred in Emery, San Juan, and/or elsewhere. Next, the statistical significance of an estimated difference refers to the likelihood that such a result comes by chance alone. In the context of synthetic control, placebo tests assess the statistical significance of an estimated effect. In the most common variant of placebo testing, used in this analysis, the analysis compares the effect of the policy switch on the unit subject to the switch (e.g. Arches or Grand County) to the effects estimated on units that were not actually subject to the switch (other parks and counties). If statistically significant, the estimated effect at the treated unit stands out against the estimated effects at untreated units. The test compares the ratio of the post-treatment MSPE to the pre-treatment MSPE for the treated unit to the corresponding ratios for untreated units, using each unit’s synthetic control as the predictor of its pre-and post- treatment outcomes. Synthetic controls of untreated units should predict post-treatment outcomes about as accurately as pre-treatment outcomes. To the extent the policy change affects the treated unit, its synthetic control should predict outcomes less accurately in the post-treatment period. A p-value measures the statistical significance of an estimated difference. In this context, the p-value equates to the percentile of the treated unit’s post-/pre-MSPE ratio among the corresponding ratios of all units. A statistically significant difference at the 5% level of significance (a traditional and standard threshold in statistics, used in this report) means no more than 5% of units have ratios as extreme as the treated unit. If the treated unit’s ratio falls solidly within the range of the untreated ratios, then the placebo test concludes that the difference is not statistically significant. Note that the magnitude required to exceed the threshold for “typical”—and so be deemed “statistically significant”—will vary by case and even differences seemingly large in a practical sense may not be large enough relative to background data variation to be statistically significant. Also, statistical significance does not imply that treatment caused the difference. 

Visitor Spending Analysis 

In this analysis, “visitor spending” includes expenditures on accommodations, auto repair, car rentals, gasoline, grocery stores, restaurants, retail, and other personal services by visitors traveling at least 50 miles (one way) to Grand County. It includes leisure and business spending by in-state and out-of-state domestic travelers, as well as international visitors. Visitor spending estimates derive from taxable sales and sales tax revenue data from the Utah State Tax Commission and visitor market share data from Visa Destination Insights. The analysis utilizes Visa data to estimate the visitor share of spending by market segment. As visitor spending flows through the local economy, it generates impacts beyond the initial “direct” amounts spent at hotels, restaurants, retail shops and other establishments. The businesses at which visitors spend their money use those dollars to pay their employees and purchase goods and services from other local businesses, who in turn do the same. These constitute “indirect” effects. The employees of the direct and indirect businesses spend a portion of their earnings in the local economy as well, generating “induced” effects. These additional rounds of indirect and induced spending, combined with the initial visitor spending, represent the total visitor spending impact. The Gardner Institute used the IMPLAN model to generate the indirect and induced effects. Fiscal impacts represent a combination of direct sales taxes calculated by the Gardner Institute and direct, indirect and induced taxes calculated by the IMPLAN model. The Gardner Institute multiplies estimated visitor expenditures by the specific state and local sales tax rates appropriate for each spending category. Analysts then add IMPLAN’s indirect and induced sales tax revenues to these amounts. The timed-entry system at Arches appears to have contributed to a positive impact on jobs in Grand County. ### [Allegheny Portage Railroad](https://www.nps.gov/alpo/)

Gallitzin, PA

The first railroad to cross the Allegheny Mountains, the Allegheny Portage Railroad was the final piece of the Pennsylvania Main Line Canal. "The Portage" opened in 1834, marking the first time that there was one, direct route between Philadelphia and Pittsburgh. All things to all people, it served merchants, passengers, slaves in pursuit of freedom, and soldiers from the Mexican War.

### [Appalachian](https://www.nps.gov/appa/)

Maine to Georgia, CT,GA,MA,MD,ME,NC,NH,NJ,NY,PA,TN,VA,VT,WV

The Appalachian Trail is a 2,190+ mile long public footpath that traverses the scenic, wooded, pastoral, wild, and culturally resonant lands of the Appalachian Mountains. Various States VA,MD,DE,DC,PA,NY

People first arrived in the Chesapeake Bay during the last ice age. As glaciers melted, diverse societies learned to thrive in a world of water. ### [Eisenhower](https://www.nps.gov/eise/)

Gettysburg, PA

Eisenhower National Historic Site preserves the farm of General and 34th President Dwight D. Eisenhower. Adjacent to the Gettysburg battlefield, the farm served the president and first lady as a weekend retreat and as a meeting place for world leaders. # National Park System

On August 25, 1916, President Woodrow Wilson signed the "Organic Act" creating the National Park Service, a federal bureau in the Department of the Interior responsible for maintaining national parks and monuments that were then managed by the department. The National Park System has since expanded to 433 units (often referred to as parks), more than 150 related areas, and numerous programs that assist in conserving the nation's natural and cultural heritage for the benefit of current and future generations.

## Units/Parks

The National Park Service manages 433 individual units covering more than 85 million acres in all 50 states, the District of Columbia, and US territories. While there are at least 19 [naming designations](https://www.nps.gov/articles/nps-designations.htm), these units are commonly referred to as "parks." Multiple parks may be managed together as an administrative unit within the National Park Service. (See more information about [recent changes in the National Park System](https://www.nps.gov/aboutus/recent-changes.htm) and [park anniversaries](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/npscelebrates/park-anniversaries.htm).)

## Related Areas

Related areas are linked in importance and purpose to places managed directly by the National Park Service by preserving important segments of the nation's natural and cultural heritage. They are designated by acts of Congress or by the Secretary of the Interior (affiliated areas). The majority of related areas are not units of the National Park Service and are managed by other government agencies or non-government organizations and landowners. The National Park Service is involved in related areas by directly managing the entire or sections of a related area, or by providing technical or financial assistance.

# National Park System

On August 25, 1916, President Woodrow Wilson signed the "Organic Act" creating the National Park Service, a federal bureau in the Department of the Interior responsible for maintaining national parks and monuments that were then managed by the department. The National Park System has since expanded to 433 units (often referred to as parks), more than 150 related areas, and numerous programs that assist in conserving the nation's natural and cultural heritage for the benefit of current and future generations.

## Units/Parks

The National Park Service manages 433 individual units covering more than 85 million acres in all 50 states, the District of Columbia, and US territories. While there are at least 19 [naming designations](https://www.nps.gov/articles/nps-designations.htm), these units are commonly referred to as "parks." Multiple parks may be managed together as an administrative unit within the National Park Service. (See more information about [recent changes in the National Park System](https://www.nps.gov/aboutus/recent-changes.htm) and [park anniversaries](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/npscelebrates/park-anniversaries.htm).)

# How Many National Parks are There?

![Image 8](https://npf-prod.imgix.net/uploads/denalinpp_sunrise_nps_karalewandowski.jpg?auto=compress%2Cformat&crop=focalpoint&fit=crop&fp-x=0.5&fp-y=0.5&h=900&q=80&w=1600)

.

Denali National Park & Preserve - NPS Photo / Kara Lewandowski

T

The National Park System encompasses **433**[national park sites](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks) in the United States. They span across more than 85 million acres, with parks in each state and extending into the territories, including parks in Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands, American Samoa, and Guam.

![Image 9: A single-story ranch-style house with light brown brick and teal siding](https://npf-prod.imgix.net/uploads/medgarandmyrlieevershomenm_nps.jpg?auto=compress%2Cformat&crop=focalpoint&fit=crop&fp-x=0.5&fp-y=0.5&h=1067&q=80&w=1600)

Medgar and Myrlie Evers Home National Monument(NPS Photo)

Within the system, there are 63 sites that include “National Park” as part of their proper name such as [Acadia](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/acadia-national-park), [Everglades](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/everglades-national-park), [Grand Canyon](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/grand-canyon-national-park), and [Yellowstone](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/yellowstone-national-park). Though world-renowned for their grandeur and beauty, our national treasures encompass far more than these 63 sites. They include landscapes and historical narratives within areas that interpret our nation’s past, and cultural and recreation areas that stretch our minds and bodies to learn and do more.

The system is comprised of 20 national park types that fall under the protection of the National Park Service to preserve, unimpaired, for this and future generations. These designations include:

**National Battlefields (11)**

A wide variety of titles are used in designations for places associated with American military history, including national battlefields, national battlefield parks, national battlefield sites, and national military parks. Other types of parks, like national monuments or national historical parks, can also include features associated with American military history.

**National Battlefield Parks (4)**

**National Battlefield Site (1)**

**National Military Parks (9)**

**National Historical Parks (63)**

![Image 10: Three benches line the corner of a covered porch](https://www.nationalparks.org/uploads/1-martinlutherkingnhp_birthhome_npf_katiebrickerphotography.jpg?itok=EzHIVrIA)

Birth Home at Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park (Katie Bricker Photography)

Places designated as national historical parks are like those designated national historic sites (see below) in that they are preserved or restored places that commemorate important persons or events in American history. However, national historical parks are commonly larger physical areas and may involve more complexity than a national historic site.

**National Historic Sites (76)**

Recently, the designation of national historic site has been the most common title Congress applies when authorizing places that commemorate persons and events important in the nation’s history as part of the National Park System. Historic areas are customarily preserved or restored to reflect their appearance during the period of their greatest historical significance, such as [Manzanar National Historic Site](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/manzanar-national-historic-site), whose reconstructed facilities help visitors get a glimpse at what life was like at the relocation center during World War II, or [Eleanor Roosevelt National Historic Site](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/eleanor-roosevelt-national-historic-site), where the furnishings of Val-Kill Cottage reflect the way the cottage appeared in the later years of Mrs. Roosevelt’s life.

**International Historic Sites (1)**

The lone international historic site, [Saint Croix Island](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/saint-croix-island-international-historic-site), refers to a site relevant to both U.S. and Canadian history.

![Image 11](https://npf-prod.imgix.net/uploads/bison_newborn-calf-yellowstone_neal-herbert_nps.jpg?auto=compress%2Cformat&fit=max&q=80&w=1600)

![Image 12: A little flow of water that drops about two feet over a rock ridge on to the rocks and Lake Superior](https://www.nationalparks.org/uploads/1-picturedrocksnl_elliotfalls_nps_william_mobilian.jpg?itok=2x376JA9)

Elliot Falls at Pictured Rocks National Lakeshore (NPS Photo / William Mobilian)

**National Lakeshores (3)**

Focused on both providing water-oriented recreation opportunities as well as the preservation of areas and offshore islands, national lakeshores can be established on any natural freshwater lake, though most are located on the Great Lakes.

**National Memorials (31)**

National memorials are primarily commemorative sites, a structure or site that marks an important event or person. Sites like [Thaddeus Kosciusko National Memorial](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/thaddeus-kosciuszko-national-memorial), the smallest unit in the National Park Service, and the iconic [Lincoln Memorial](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/lincoln-memorial) in the nation’s capital, honor the life and legacy of individuals, while sites like [De Soto National Memorial](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/de-soto-national-memorial) and [Flight 93 National Memorial](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/flight-93-national-memorial) commemorate a specific event.

**National Monuments (87)**

Sites designated as national monuments are usually smaller than a national park. Intended to preserve at least one nationally significant resource, such as [Aztec Ruins National Monument](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/aztec-ruins-national-monument), which preserves a 900-year-old ancestral Pueblo Great House in New Mexico, California’s [Lava Beds National Monument](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/lava-beds-national-monument), which protects the land shaped by the Medicine Lake volcano, or [Pullman National Monument](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/pullman-national-monument) in Chicago, which preserves the story of one of the first planned industrial communities.

**National Parks (63)**

Generally, a national park contains a variety of resources, encompassing large areas of land or water. Their designation as a national park helps provide adequate protection of the area’s resources, and enforces restrictions on the public’s use of the lands to maintain the park’s resources.

**National Parkways (4)**

Ribbons of land flanking roadways and offering scenic views are designated national parkways. Though there are four national parkways currently in the National Park System, other units also include parkways within their park boundaries.

**National Preserves (19)**

Established for the protection of certain resources, national preserves have less restrictions on the use of the lands than national parks, as long as the activities do not disturb the land’s natural values. [Big Cypress](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/big-cypress-national-preserve) and [Big Thicket](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/big-thicket-national-preserve) were the first authorized national preserves, designated in 1974.

**National Reserves (2)**

Similar to national preserves (above), national reserves protect certain resources as well. However, management of national reserves like [City of Rocks](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/city-rocks-national-reserve) may be transferred to local or state authorities.

![Image 13: cactus like tree to left, mountains cloudy sky behind](https://www.nationalparks.org/uploads/1-lakemeadnra_joshuatreeforest_nps_andrewcattoir.jpg?itok=bX0pITQg)

Joshua tree forest at Lake Mead National Recreation Area (NPS Photo / Andrew Cattoir)

**National Recreation Areas (18)**

Originally units that were surrounding reservoirs impounded by dams built by other federal agencies, the concept of a national recreation area has grown to encompass other land and water areas set aside for recreational use by acts of Congress. Some of the first national recreation areas, like [Chickasaw](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/chickasaw-national-recreation-area), were managed by NPS under cooperative agreements. Today, there are also national recreation areas like [Hells Canyon](https://www.fs.usda.gov/detail/wallowa-whitman/recreation/?cid=stelprdb5238987) and [Sawtooth](https://www.fs.usda.gov/sawtooth) that are administered by the Forest Service, part of the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

**National Rivers (4)**

Sites designated as national rivers preserve free-flowing streams and their immediate environment with at least one remarkable natural, cultural, or recreational value. National rivers and sites designated as wild and scenic riverways (see below) must naturally flow without major alteration of the waterway and provide recreational opportunities like canoeing and hiking.

**National Scenic Trails (6)**

National scenic trails are generally long-distance footpaths winding through areas of natural beauty. Five of the six national scenic trails run through multiple states, with the [Appalachian National Scenic Trail](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/appalachian-national-scenic-trail) covering 14 states!

![Image 14: Four white-sided, red-roofed structures sit on a rocky headland above the Pacific Ocean at the base of a long stairway. Above and to the left of the lighthouse, the sun filters through wispy clouds as it descends toward the horizon.](https://npf-prod.imgix.net/uploads/PointReyesNS_LighthouseatSunset_NPS_AnelaRamosKopshever.jpeg?auto=compress%2Cformat&crop=focalpoint&fit=crop&fp-x=0.5&fp-y=0.5&h=1067&q=80&w=1600)

Point Reyes Lighthouse at Point Reyes National Seashore(NPS Photo / Anela Ramos Kopshever)

**National Seashores (10)**

Like national lakeshores, national seashores preserve shoreline areas and offshore islands. Located on the Atlantic, Gulf, and Pacific coasts, national seashores preserve natural resources while providing visitors with on-the-water fun.

**National Wild and Scenic Rivers and Riverways (10)**

Like national rivers, national wild and scenic rivers and riverways preserve both the naturally flowing streams and their immediate environment. National wild and scenic rivers and riverways, like [Bluestone National Scenic River](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/bluestone-national-scenic-river) in West Virginia and Tennessee’s [Obed Wild & Scenic River](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/obed-wild-and-scenic-river) have great natural and cultural value, and their designation preserves both the natural resources around the river and stories of those who lived and worked along the rivers.

**Other Designations (11)**

Though it may seem like the designations listed above cover every site, there are special sites within the National Park System that are designated otherwise. Places like [Wolf Trap National Park for the Performing Arts](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/wolf-trap-national-park-performing-arts), the parks along our [National Mall and Memorial Parks](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/national-mall-and-memorial-parks), and even the [White House](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/white-house-and-presidents-park) fall into this “other designations” category.

Discover the wonder of a national park near you – with over 430 places for you to [find your park](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks), there is always something new to explore! These places belong to us all, and we all have a place in them. The National Park Foundation is committed to ensure that more people can discover their own connections to our parks, because national parks don’t just stand for where America has been – [they inspire where we go next](https://www.nationalparks.org/connect/blog/wonder-calls-our-national-parks).

# How Many National Parks are There?

![Image 8](https://npf-prod.imgix.net/uploads/denalinpp_sunrise_nps_karalewandowski.jpg?auto=compress%2Cformat&crop=focalpoint&fit=crop&fp-x=0.5&fp-y=0.5&h=900&q=80&w=1600)

.

Denali National Park & Preserve - NPS Photo / Kara Lewandowski

T

The National Park System encompasses **433**[national park sites](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks) in the United States. They span across more than 85 million acres, with parks in each state and extending into the territories, including parks in Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands, American Samoa, and Guam.

![Image 9: A single-story ranch-style house with light brown brick and teal siding](https://npf-prod.imgix.net/uploads/medgarandmyrlieevershomenm_nps.jpg?auto=compress%2Cformat&crop=focalpoint&fit=crop&fp-x=0.5&fp-y=0.5&h=1067&q=80&w=1600)

Medgar and Myrlie Evers Home National Monument(NPS Photo)

Within the system, there are 63 sites that include “National Park” as part of their proper name such as [Acadia](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/acadia-national-park), [Everglades](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/everglades-national-park), [Grand Canyon](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/grand-canyon-national-park), and [Yellowstone](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/yellowstone-national-park). Though world-renowned for their grandeur and beauty, our national treasures encompass far more than these 63 sites. They include landscapes and historical narratives within areas that interpret our nation’s past, and cultural and recreation areas that stretch our minds and bodies to learn and do more.

The system is comprised of 20 national park types that fall under the protection of the National Park Service to preserve, unimpaired, for this and future generations. These designations include:

**National Battlefields (11)**

A wide variety of titles are used in designations for places associated with American military history, including national battlefields, national battlefield parks, national battlefield sites, and national military parks. Other types of parks, like national monuments or national historical parks, can also include features associated with American military history.

**National Battlefield Parks (4)**

**National Battlefield Site (1)**

**National Military Parks (9)**

**National Historical Parks (63)**

![Image 10: Three benches line the corner of a covered porch](https://www.nationalparks.org/uploads/1-martinlutherkingnhp_birthhome_npf_katiebrickerphotography.jpg?itok=EzHIVrIA)

Birth Home at Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park (Katie Bricker Photography)

Places designated as national historical parks are like those designated national historic sites (see below) in that they are preserved or restored places that commemorate important persons or events in American history. However, national historical parks are commonly larger physical areas and may involve more complexity than a national historic site.

**National Historic Sites (76)**

Recently, the designation of national historic site has been the most common title Congress applies when authorizing places that commemorate persons and events important in the nation’s history as part of the National Park System. Historic areas are customarily preserved or restored to reflect their appearance during the period of their greatest historical significance, such as [Manzanar National Historic Site](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/manzanar-national-historic-site), whose reconstructed facilities help visitors get a glimpse at what life was like at the relocation center during World War II, or [Eleanor Roosevelt National Historic Site](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/eleanor-roosevelt-national-historic-site), where the furnishings of Val-Kill Cottage reflect the way the cottage appeared in the later years of Mrs. Roosevelt’s life.

**International Historic Sites (1)**

The lone international historic site, [Saint Croix Island](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/saint-croix-island-international-historic-site), refers to a site relevant to both U.S. and Canadian history.

![Image 11](https://npf-prod.imgix.net/uploads/bison_newborn-calf-yellowstone_neal-herbert_nps.jpg?auto=compress%2Cformat&fit=max&q=80&w=1600)

**National Lakeshores (3)**

Focused on both providing water-oriented recreation opportunities as well as the preservation of areas and offshore islands, national lakeshores can be established on any natural freshwater lake, though most are located on the Great Lakes.

**National Memorials (31)**

National memorials are primarily commemorative sites, a structure or site that marks an important event or person. Sites like [Thaddeus Kosciusko National Memorial](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/thaddeus-kosciuszko-national-memorial), the smallest unit in the National Park Service, and the iconic [Lincoln Memorial](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/lincoln-memorial) in the nation’s capital, honor the life and legacy of individuals, while sites like [De Soto National Memorial](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/de-soto-national-memorial) and [Flight 93 National Memorial](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/flight-93-national-memorial) commemorate a specific event.

**National Monuments (87)**

Sites designated as national monuments are usually smaller than a national park. Intended to preserve at least one nationally significant resource, such as [Aztec Ruins National Monument](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/aztec-ruins-national-monument), which preserves a 900-year-old ancestral Pueblo Great House in New Mexico, California’s [Lava Beds National Monument](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/lava-beds-national-monument), which protects the land shaped by the Medicine Lake volcano, or [Pullman National Monument](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/pullman-national-monument) in Chicago, which preserves the story of one of the first planned industrial communities.

**National Parks (63)**

Generally, a national park contains a variety of resources, encompassing large areas of land or water. Their designation as a national park helps provide adequate protection of the area’s resources, and enforces restrictions on the public’s use of the lands to maintain the park’s resources.

**National Parkways (4)**

Ribbons of land flanking roadways and offering scenic views are designated national parkways. Though there are four national parkways currently in the National Park System, other units also include parkways within their park boundaries.

**National Preserves (19)**

Established for the protection of certain resources, national preserves have less restrictions on the use of the lands than national parks, as long as the activities do not disturb the land’s natural values. [Big Cypress](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/big-cypress-national-preserve) and [Big Thicket](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/big-thicket-national-preserve) were the first authorized national preserves, designated in 1974.

**National Reserves (2)**

Similar to national preserves (above), national reserves protect certain resources as well. However, management of national reserves like [City of Rocks](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/city-rocks-national-reserve) may be transferred to local or state authorities.

![Image 13: cactus like tree to left, mountains cloudy sky behind](https://www.nationalparks.org/uploads/1-lakemeadnra_joshuatreeforest_nps_andrewcattoir.jpg?itok=bX0pITQg)

Joshua tree forest at Lake Mead National Recreation Area (NPS Photo / Andrew Cattoir)

**National Recreation Areas (18)**

Originally units that were surrounding reservoirs impounded by dams built by other federal agencies, the concept of a national recreation area has grown to encompass other land and water areas set aside for recreational use by acts of Congress. Some of the first national recreation areas, like [Chickasaw](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/chickasaw-national-recreation-area), were managed by NPS under cooperative agreements. Today, there are also national recreation areas like [Hells Canyon](https://www.fs.usda.gov/detail/wallowa-whitman/recreation/?cid=stelprdb5238987) and [Sawtooth](https://www.fs.usda.gov/sawtooth) that are administered by the Forest Service, part of the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

**National Rivers (4)**

Sites designated as national rivers preserve free-flowing streams and their immediate environment with at least one remarkable natural, cultural, or recreational value. National rivers and sites designated as wild and scenic riverways (see below) must naturally flow without major alteration of the waterway and provide recreational opportunities like canoeing and hiking.

**National Scenic Trails (6)**

National scenic trails are generally long-distance footpaths winding through areas of natural beauty. Five of the six national scenic trails run through multiple states, with the [Appalachian National Scenic Trail](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/appalachian-national-scenic-trail) covering 14 states!

![Image 14: Four white-sided, red-roofed structures sit on a rocky headland above the Pacific Ocean at the base of a long stairway. Above and to the left of the lighthouse, the sun filters through wispy clouds as it descends toward the horizon.](https://npf-prod.imgix.net/uploads/PointReyesNS_LighthouseatSunset_NPS_AnelaRamosKopshever.jpeg?auto=compress%2Cformat&crop=focalpoint&fit=crop&fp-x=0.5&fp-y=0.5&h=1067&q=80&w=1600)

Point Reyes Lighthouse at Point Reyes National Seashore(NPS Photo / Anela Ramos Kopshever)

**National Seashores (10)**

Like national lakeshores, national seashores preserve shoreline areas and offshore islands. Located on the Atlantic, Gulf, and Pacific coasts, national seashores preserve natural resources while providing visitors with on-the-water fun.

**National Wild and Scenic Rivers and Riverways (10)**

Like national rivers, national wild and scenic rivers and riverways preserve both the naturally flowing streams and their immediate environment. National wild and scenic rivers and riverways, like [Bluestone National Scenic River](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/bluestone-national-scenic-river) in West Virginia and Tennessee’s [Obed Wild & Scenic River](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/obed-wild-and-scenic-river) have great natural and cultural value, and their designation preserves both the natural resources around the river and stories of those who lived and worked along the rivers.

**Other Designations (11)**

Though it may seem like the designations listed above cover every site, there are special sites within the National Park System that are designated otherwise. Places like [Wolf Trap National Park for the Performing Arts](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/wolf-trap-national-park-performing-arts), the parks along our [National Mall and Memorial Parks](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/national-mall-and-memorial-parks), and even the [White House](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks/white-house-and-presidents-park) fall into this “other designations” category.

Discover the wonder of a national park near you – with over 430 places for you to [find your park](https://www.nationalparks.org/explore-parks), there is always something new to explore! These places belong to us all, and we all have a place in them. The National Park Foundation is committed to ensure that more people can discover their own connections to our parks, because national parks don’t just stand for where America has been – [they inspire where we go next](https://www.nationalparks.org/connect/blog/wonder-calls-our-national-parks).

# National Parks in Pennsylvania

**There are 18 national park service sites in Pennsylvania.**Discover what makes each site of cultural and historical importance below:

![Image 4: NPS Sites Pennsylvania Placeholder](https://everything-everywhere.com/wp-content/plugins/interactive-world-maps/imgs/placeholder.png)  
NPS Sites Pennsylvania

    *   Allegheny Portage Railroad National Historic Site

*       *   Hopewell Furnace National Historic Site

    *   Upper Delaware Scenic and Recreational River
    *   Valley Forge National Historical Park

* * *

## Allegheny Portage Railroad National Historic Site

Whether you are a history buff or a train enthusiast, the Allegheny Portage Railroad National Historic Site is a must-visit. As one of the national park service sites in Pennsylvania, it is governed and managed by the US NPS. This site showcases the railroad history of the nation, which commemorates the Allegheny Portage Railroad (the first railroad ever constructed within the Allegheny Mountains).

The railroad is built on an inclined plane somewhere between the early to the mid-19th century. During that time, the railroad was considered a technological feat. The railroad opened up channels for trade and settlement in this part of the United States.

## Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area

This 70,000-acre property is one of the national park service sites in Pennsylvania and was established to preserve a protected area near the Delaware River. This site is located somewhere between Pennsylvania and New Jersey. A 40-mile section of the Delaware River is included in the national recreation area’s premises and is also granted protected status.

The national recreation area was established in 1978 and offers both cultural and historical sites. Meanwhile, the Native American archaeological sites are probably the one that garners the most interest. For those who are into outdoor recreational activities, there are plenty of options in the property such as hiking, swimming, camping, cycling, canoeing, and picnicking, to name a few.

## Edgar Allan Poe National Historic Site

This historic site is focused on preserving a home that was once rented by the famous American author, Edgar Allan Poe. The house is located in Spring Garden, Philadelphia. Aside from this house, Poe lived in Philadelphia for a long time. This house is the only one that survived out of all of them. The original house was built in 1842 but the site was listed into the National Register of Historic Places in 1966.

## Eisenhower National Historic Site

This property encompasses a home and farm in Adams County, Pennsylvania. The house and the farm are important because this is where the 34th US President Dwight Eisenhower lived for many years. The entire property consists of over 690 acres of land area and served as a retreat for the President for the weekends. Meanwhile, he also hosted several other leaders for a meeting in this farm. When Eisenhower ended his term as a President in 1961, he lived in the house and farm.

## First State National Historical Park

This unit of the National Park Service is located in Chadds Ford, which was initially designated by a national monument by President Barack Obama in 2013. It was later elevated into national historical park status by the Congress.

The property covers the early colonial history of Delaware and how it played a role in the establishment of the nation, which led to it being named as the first state. It follows the story of early settlers such as Swedes, Finns, Dutch and English and how they interacted with the Native American tribes.

## Flight 93 National Memorial

This national memorial site is also the same crash site of United Airlines Flight 93 that was hijacked during the September 11 attacks. The site of the crash is in Somerset County, Pennsylvania. The memorial was established to honor the memory of the passengers and crew of Flight 93, who fought the hijackers in order to prevent the terrorists from reaching their target.

A visitor center was established in September 2015. It is located on a hill with an overlooking view of the memorial site. Within the memorial site is a white marble Wall of Names for all of the victims. Both the visitor center and the memorial site are beneath the path of Flight 93 when it crashed on the area.

## Fort Necessity National Battlefield

Located in Fayette Country, this battlefield site is one of the national park service sites in Pennsylvania. The property aims to preserve the site of the Battle of Fort Necessity that took place in 1754 between the French and Indians. Also included in the site is Mount Washington Tavern, which is located along the National Road. The site was established in 1931 but it wasn’t until 1933 when the National Park Service managed the site.

## Friendship Hill National Historic Site

This is another site maintained and managed by the National Park Service. It was the home of Albert Gallatin, who is an early American politician and statesman. He served as a Secretary of Treasury under two Presidential terms. He also served as an ambassador to other countries such as France and Great Britain.

There are several sections that make up the house. The original Federalist-style brick house built in the 18th century is the primary feature of this historic site. In 1798, a simple frame dwelling was constructed as another unit of the brick house. Other structures followed namely the Stone House, a three-and-a-half story structure, a stone kitchen, State Dining Room, and servant’s quarters.

## Gettysburg National Military Park

The Battle of Gettysburg is written a lot about in history books. Hence, this site is one of the most important sites during the American Civil War era. Named as one of the national park service sites in Pennsylvania, Gettysburg National Military Park is located in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. There are several properties included within the park such as Gettysburg Battlefield, Gettysburg National Cemetery, Gettysburg Museum and Visitor Center, and several other non-battle areas. The park receives more than 1 million tourist visits each year. In 1915, a school for licensing tour guides to Gettysburg was established.

## Hopewell Furnace National Historic Site

Located in Elverson, Pennsylvania, this historic site is preserved as it is believed to be the best example of a rural “iron plantation” in America. It has been around since the 19th century and is comprised of many buildings such as the blast furnace, ironmaster’s house, blacksmith shop, workers’ houses, and many other auxiliary buildings. Hopewell Furnace was established in the late 18th century by ironmaster Mark Bird. It was from 1820 to 1840 when this site experienced a major boom, particularly due to the American Civil War activity. By the mid-19th century, newer methods of ironmaking were introduced until the methods used by Hopewell Furnace were rendered obsolete. In 1883, the site was no longer in operation.

## Independence National Historical Park

![Image 5: national park service sites in Pennsylvania](https://photos.smugmug.com/North-America/Pennsylvania/Philadelphia/i-CvL39mz/1/K954vKbjWnNs9T8n6649NbjZDKp6d2DGxttrM3fk4/XL/_GMA5636_tonemapped-XL.jpg)

There are several sites included in this listing for national park service sites in Pennsylvania. The Independence Hall, a [UNESCO World Heritage Site](https://everything-everywhere.com/unesco-world-heritage-site-115-independence-hall/), is the main feature of this historical park. This is where the Declaration of Independence and US Constitution were established.

Aside from the Independence Hall, the Liberty Bell is another important feature of this historical park. Other historic buildings found in the park are First Bank of the United States, Carpenters’ Hall, and the City Tavern (which is a recreation of the colonial tavern that delegates from the US Congress frequented during the 18th century).

## Johnstown Flood National Memorial

This site was established to commemorate the 2,200 people who died during a flood in Johnstown, Pennsylvania. The site was established in 1964 and covers more than 164 acres in land area. The flood took place in 1889 and was caused when the South Fork Dam collapsed. Meanwhile, the memorial itself is located in 733 Lake Road. In addition to the memorial, the site also aims to preserve what was left of the dam.

## Middle Delaware National Scenic River

The Delaware River is one of the largest free-flowing rivers without a dam or other control structures in the United States. And yet, the water quality in the river is considered exceptional. This scenic river stretches for 40 miles and forms the boundary between Pennsylvania and New Jersey. Along the path of the river are forested mountains, as well as a mountain ridge more commonly referred to as “Water Gap”.

## Potomac Heritage Trail

This property connects various trails and sites of historical importance in the supper southeast region of the US. It covers the natural, cultural and historical features of the properties covered along this trail route. Unlike the Appalachian Trails and other long distance hiking trails, there are numerous alternative routes and side trails to explore.

## Steamtown National Historic Site

The Steamtown National Historic Site in Scranton is one of the national park service sites in Pennsylvania. It is a railroad museum and heritage railroad in one. The site of the museum is the former location of the Scranton yards. The entire museum is built on a turntable and roundhouse, which are replications of the original DL&W facilities. The railroad equipment and locomotives that are on display at this national historic site were part of the collection of F. Nelson Blount.

## Thaddeus Kosciuszko National Memorial

This memorial is located in 301 Pine Street in Philadelphia. The main feature of the memorial site is the home of Thaddeus Kosciuszko, who is a Polish patriot and hero during the time of the American Civil War. The memorial site commemorates the life and works of the Polish hero. When he was wounded, captured and imprisoned from his native Poland that was ruled by Russia in the late 18th century, he went to the United States. He instructed his secretary to find a small and cheap boarding house, which is the current home preserved in the memorial. This is where he spent most of his time in as he recuperated from his wounds. The site was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1970.

The memorial site is currently open for tours; no fees or reservations are required.

## Upper Delaware Scenic and Recreational River

This scenic and recreational area is part of the stretch of the Delaware River. It starts from Narrowsburg, New York and passes along Lackawaxen, Pennsylvania, passing through five counties in total. Also included in the site is the Zane Grey Museum and Roebling’s Delaware Aqueduct. The Zane Grey Museum is being preserved after it sustained a lot of damage due to the 2006 flood in the Eastern part of the United States. Even though the NPS is the governing body for this site, most of the land within the area is privately-owned.

## Valley Forge National Historical Park

This historical park is listed as one of the national park service sites in Pennsylvania and protects the site of third winter encampment by the Continental Army during the Revolutionary War in America. The encampment lasted for 6 months in the late 18th century. The total land area of the park is more than 3,500 acres. Over 1.2 million people also visit this park each year.

Within the historical park, there are restored historic structures or reconstructed buildings. There are also monuments within the park built to commemorate the key players of the American Revolutionary War. A visitor center and museum are available on-site wherein there are showcases of artifacts and historical emblems.

# National Parks in Pennsylvania

**There are 18 national park service sites in Pennsylvania.**Discover what makes each site of cultural and historical importance below:

![Image 4: NPS Sites Pennsylvania Placeholder](https://everything-everywhere.com/wp-content/plugins/interactive-world-maps/imgs/placeholder.png)

* * *

## Allegheny Portage Railroad National Historic Site

Whether you are a history buff or a train enthusiast, the Allegheny Portage Railroad National Historic Site is a must-visit. As one of the national park service sites in Pennsylvania, it is governed and managed by the US NPS. This site showcases the railroad history of the nation, which commemorates the Allegheny Portage Railroad (the first railroad ever constructed within the Allegheny Mountains).

The railroad is built on an inclined plane somewhere between the early to the mid-19th century. During that time, the railroad was considered a technological feat. The railroad opened up channels for trade and settlement in this part of the United States.

## Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area

This 70,000-acre property is one of the national park service sites in Pennsylvania and was established to preserve a protected area near the Delaware River. This site is located somewhere between Pennsylvania and New Jersey. A 40-mile section of the Delaware River is included in the national recreation area’s premises and is also granted protected status.

The national recreation area was established in 1978 and offers both cultural and historical sites. Meanwhile, the Native American archaeological sites are probably the one that garners the most interest. For those who are into outdoor recreational activities, there are plenty of options in the property such as hiking, swimming, camping, cycling, canoeing, and picnicking, to name a few.

## Edgar Allan Poe National Historic Site

This historic site is focused on preserving a home that was once rented by the famous American author, Edgar Allan Poe. The house is located in Spring Garden, Philadelphia. Aside from this house, Poe lived in Philadelphia for a long time. This house is the only one that survived out of all of them. The original house was built in 1842 but the site was listed into the National Register of Historic Places in 1966.

## Eisenhower National Historic Site

This property encompasses a home and farm in Adams County, Pennsylvania. The house and the farm are important because this is where the 34th US President Dwight Eisenhower lived for many years. The entire property consists of over 690 acres of land area and served as a retreat for the President for the weekends. Meanwhile, he also hosted several other leaders for a meeting in this farm. When Eisenhower ended his term as a President in 1961, he lived in the house and farm.

## First State National Historical Park

This unit of the National Park Service is located in Chadds Ford, which was initially designated by a national monument by President Barack Obama in 2013. It was later elevated into national historical park status by the Congress.

The property covers the early colonial history of Delaware and how it played a role in the establishment of the nation, which led to it being named as the first state. It follows the story of early settlers such as Swedes, Finns, Dutch and English and how they interacted with the Native American tribes.

## Flight 93 National Memorial

This national memorial site is also the same crash site of United Airlines Flight 93 that was hijacked during the September 11 attacks. The site of the crash is in Somerset County, Pennsylvania. The memorial was established to honor the memory of the passengers and crew of Flight 93, who fought the hijackers in order to prevent the terrorists from reaching their target.

A visitor center was established in September 2015. It is located on a hill with an overlooking view of the memorial site. Within the memorial site is a white marble Wall of Names for all of the victims. Both the visitor center and the memorial site are beneath the path of Flight 93 when it crashed on the area.

## Fort Necessity National Battlefield

Located in Fayette Country, this battlefield site is one of the national park service sites in Pennsylvania. The property aims to preserve the site of the Battle of Fort Necessity that took place in 1754 between the French and Indians. Also included in the site is Mount Washington Tavern, which is located along the National Road. The site was established in 1931 but it wasn’t until 1933 when the National Park Service managed the site.

## Friendship Hill National Historic Site

This is another site maintained and managed by the National Park Service. It was the home of Albert Gallatin, who is an early American politician and statesman. He served as a Secretary of Treasury under two Presidential terms. He also served as an ambassador to other countries such as France and Great Britain.

There are several sections that make up the house. The original Federalist-style brick house built in the 18th century is the primary feature of this historic site. In 1798, a simple frame dwelling was constructed as another unit of the brick house. Other structures followed namely the Stone House, a three-and-a-half story structure, a stone kitchen, State Dining Room, and servant’s quarters.

## Gettysburg National Military Park

The Battle of Gettysburg is written a lot about in history books. Hence, this site is one of the most important sites during the American Civil War era. Named as one of the national park service sites in Pennsylvania, Gettysburg National Military Park is located in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. There are several properties included within the park such as Gettysburg Battlefield, Gettysburg National Cemetery, Gettysburg Museum and Visitor Center, and several other non-battle areas. The park receives more than 1 million tourist visits each year. In 1915, a school for licensing tour guides to Gettysburg was established.

## Hopewell Furnace National Historic Site

Located in Elverson, Pennsylvania, this historic site is preserved as it is believed to be the best example of a rural “iron plantation” in America. It has been around since the 19th century and is comprised of many buildings such as the blast furnace, ironmaster’s house, blacksmith shop, workers’ houses, and many other auxiliary buildings. Hopewell Furnace was established in the late 18th century by ironmaster Mark Bird. It was from 1820 to 1840 when this site experienced a major boom, particularly due to the American Civil War activity. By the mid-19th century, newer methods of ironmaking were introduced until the methods used by Hopewell Furnace were rendered obsolete. In 1883, the site was no longer in operation.

## Independence National Historical Park

![Image 5: national park service sites in Pennsylvania](https://photos.smugmug.com/North-America/Pennsylvania/Philadelphia/i-CvL39mz/1/K954vKbjWnNs9T8n6649NbjZDKp6d2DGxttrM3fk4/XL/_GMA5636_tonemapped-XL.jpg)

There are several sites included in this listing for national park service sites in Pennsylvania. The Independence Hall, a [UNESCO World Heritage Site](https://everything-everywhere.com/unesco-world-heritage-site-115-independence-hall/), is the main feature of this historical park. This is where the Declaration of Independence and US Constitution were established.

Aside from the Independence Hall, the Liberty Bell is another important feature of this historical park. Other historic buildings found in the park are First Bank of the United States, Carpenters’ Hall, and the City Tavern (which is a recreation of the colonial tavern that delegates from the US Congress frequented during the 18th century).

## Johnstown Flood National Memorial

This site was established to commemorate the 2,200 people who died during a flood in Johnstown, Pennsylvania. The site was established in 1964 and covers more than 164 acres in land area. The flood took place in 1889 and was caused when the South Fork Dam collapsed. Meanwhile, the memorial itself is located in 733 Lake Road. In addition to the memorial, the site also aims to preserve what was left of the dam.

## Middle Delaware National Scenic River

The Delaware River is one of the largest free-flowing rivers without a dam or other control structures in the United States. And yet, the water quality in the river is considered exceptional. This scenic river stretches for 40 miles and forms the boundary between Pennsylvania and New Jersey. Along the path of the river are forested mountains, as well as a mountain ridge more commonly referred to as “Water Gap”.

## Potomac Heritage Trail

This property connects various trails and sites of historical importance in the supper southeast region of the US. It covers the natural, cultural and historical features of the properties covered along this trail route. Unlike the Appalachian Trails and other long distance hiking trails, there are numerous alternative routes and side trails to explore.

## Steamtown National Historic Site

The Steamtown National Historic Site in Scranton is one of the national park service sites in Pennsylvania. It is a railroad museum and heritage railroad in one. The site of the museum is the former location of the Scranton yards. The entire museum is built on a turntable and roundhouse, which are replications of the original DL&W facilities. The railroad equipment and locomotives that are on display at this national historic site were part of the collection of F. Nelson Blount.

## Thaddeus Kosciuszko National Memorial

This memorial is located in 301 Pine Street in Philadelphia. The main feature of the memorial site is the home of Thaddeus Kosciuszko, who is a Polish patriot and hero during the time of the American Civil War. The memorial site commemorates the life and works of the Polish hero. When he was wounded, captured and imprisoned from his native Poland that was ruled by Russia in the late 18th century, he went to the United States. He instructed his secretary to find a small and cheap boarding house, which is the current home preserved in the memorial. This is where he spent most of his time in as he recuperated from his wounds. The site was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1970.

The memorial site is currently open for tours; no fees or reservations are required.

## Upper Delaware Scenic and Recreational River

This scenic and recreational area is part of the stretch of the Delaware River. It starts from Narrowsburg, New York and passes along Lackawaxen, Pennsylvania, passing through five counties in total. Also included in the site is the Zane Grey Museum and Roebling’s Delaware Aqueduct. The Zane Grey Museum is being preserved after it sustained a lot of damage due to the 2006 flood in the Eastern part of the United States. Even though the NPS is the governing body for this site, most of the land within the area is privately-owned.

## Valley Forge National Historical Park

This historical park is listed as one of the national park service sites in Pennsylvania and protects the site of third winter encampment by the Continental Army during the Revolutionary War in America. The encampment lasted for 6 months in the late 18th century. The total land area of the park is more than 3,500 acres. Over 1.2 million people also visit this park each year.

Within the historical park, there are restored historic structures or reconstructed buildings. There are also monuments within the park built to commemorate the key players of the American Revolutionary War. A visitor center and museum are available on-site wherein there are showcases of artifacts and historical emblems.

# Printable list of National Parks Sites in the United States (433 sites)

Printable list of National Parks Sites including all 433 National Parks, Seashores, Historic Sites, and more! Check off how many you have been to!

Did you know that the US National Park Sites include:

63 US National Parks  
87 US [National Monuments](https://www.parkrangerjohn.com/us-national-monuments/)  
19 US National Preserves  
63 US [National Historical Parks](https://www.parkrangerjohn.com/us-national-historical-parks/)  
76 US [National Historic Sites](https://www.parkrangerjohn.com/us-national-historic-sites/)  
1 US International Historic Site  
4 US National Battlefield Parks  
9 US National Military Parks  
11 US National Battlefields  
1 National Battlefield Site  
31 [National Memorials](https://www.parkrangerjohn.com/us-national-memorials/)  
18 National Recreation Areas  
10 [National Seashores](https://www.parkrangerjohn.com/us-national-seashores/)  
3 National Lake Shores  
4 National Rivers  
10 National Wild and Scenic Rivers and Riverways  
2 National Reserves  
4 National Parkways  
6 National Scenic Trails  
11 other sites including the National Mall and National Capital Parks

For a total of 433

Some of the sites listed are not included in the 433 count but are managed or influenced by the National Park Service. These sites are listed below each state as affiliated sites.

These are sites that the National Park service helps run, provides grant money, staffing, or overview of. They are often co-managed with other groups to provide the best services and information for visitors.

# Printable list of National Parks Sites in the United States (433 sites)

Printable list of National Parks Sites including all 433 National Parks, Seashores, Historic Sites, and more! Check off how many you have been to!

Did you know that the US National Park Sites include:

63 US National Parks  
87 US [National Monuments](https://www.parkrangerjohn.com/us-national-monuments/)  
19 US National Preserves  
63 US [National Historical Parks](https://www.parkrangerjohn.com/us-national-historical-parks/)

1 US International Historic Site  
4 US National Battlefield Parks  
9 US National Military Parks  
11 US National Battlefields  
1 National Battlefield Site  
31 [National Memorials](https://www.parkrangerjohn.com/us-national-memorials/)  
18 National Recreation Areas  
10 [National Seashores](https://www.parkrangerjohn.com/us-national-seashores/)  
3 National Lake Shores  
4 National Rivers  
10 National Wild and Scenic Rivers and Riverways  
2 National Reserves  
4 National Parkways  
6 National Scenic Trails  
11 other sites including the National Mall and National Capital Parks

For a total of 433

Some of the sites listed are not included in the 433 count but are managed or influenced by the National Park Service. These sites are listed below each state as affiliated sites.

These are sites that the National Park service helps run, provides grant money, staffing, or overview of. They are often co-managed with other groups to provide the best services and information for visitors.

The logo of the [National Park Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service "National Park Service")

The **Official Units of the National Park System** of the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") is the collection of physical properties owned or administered by the [National Park Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service "National Park Service").

As of December 2024, there are 433 official units of the [National Park System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service#National_Park_System "National Park Service");[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_the_United_States_National_Park_System_official_units#cite_note-1) however, this number can be misleading. For example, [Denali National Park and Preserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denali_National_Park_and_Preserve "Denali National Park and Preserve") are counted as two units, since the same name applies to a national park and an adjacent national preserve. Yet [Jean Lafitte National Historical Park and Preserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Lafitte_National_Historical_Park_and_Preserve "Jean Lafitte National Historical Park and Preserve") is counted as one unit, despite its double designation. Counting methodology is rooted in the language of a park's enabling legislation. Furthermore, the NPS contributes resources to "affiliated areas" which do not fall under its administration, and these do not count toward the official list number. An example is [Oklahoma City National Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_City_National_Memorial "Oklahoma City National Memorial").

These units are a subset of the [areas in the United States National Park System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_areas_in_the_United_States_National_Park_System "List of areas in the United States National Park System"), and nearly all participate in the [national park passport stamps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_park_passport_stamps "National park passport stamps") program. National Park System units are found in all 50 states, in the [District of Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), and in the [U.S. territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insular_area "Insular area") of [Guam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guam "Guam"), [American Samoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Samoa "American Samoa"), the [U.S. Virgin Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Virgin_Islands "United States Virgin Islands"), and [Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rico "Puerto Rico"). (The territory of the [Northern Mariana Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Mariana_Islands "Northern Mariana Islands") has an affiliated area but not an official NPS unit.)
